An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). This measure surpasses previous findings from CDF and D0 and contributes to the determination of $B^0_s$ lifetime with an uncertainty of 0.0065 picoseconds. Additionally, the branching fraction of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ was measured at (0.097 ± 0.003 stat. ± 0.002 syst.) × 10^-4. A 1.5σ deviation from this measure with respect to theoretical predictions made by the Global Fit group has been observed. The contribution to the uncertainty from this measure alone is negligible. The measured value of $B^0\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time, obtained in a previous LHCb study, has been confirmed and found consistent with the new $B^0_s$ result. The measured values of $B^0_s$ and $B^0$ effective lifetimes differ by 0.027 picoseconds. Two exotic models have been ruled out by more than 2 orders of magnitude and the measured values provide more stringent constraints on models that influence the $B^0_s$ system at a level of 10^-3 × (1.44 ps)^4. The most influential of these models is the Standard Model plus a single operator contributing to the $b\rightarrow s\ell^+\ell^-$ process. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$, whose metrics also appear in certain infinite series of $\theta$. The matrices $E_{ab}$ can be represented in simple forms for certain algebras like $su(2)$ and $u(N)$. Additionally, our study has yielded new nonstandard metric formulas for all the spheres $S^n$, projective spaces $RP^n$, and $U(2)$. The notable $su(2)$ algebra allows for a straightforward physical interpretation, where the noncommutative space represents a novel three-dimensional sphere with a curvature determined by the deformation parameter $\theta$. A similar relationship holds for the $so(3)$ and $so(4)$ algebras. A direct connection exists between the ratio $\theta/p$ and the effective noncommutative parameter $\theta_{eff} = \theta p^2$ in the classical limit, leading to a reevaluation of previous works. The new understanding offers a flexible path to explore real values of the deformation parameter. Finally, this study provides valuable insights that can be applied to other nonlinear algebras. A comparison between different parameterization of the su(2) algebra is also included in the supplementary materials. The proposed approach can be applied to any Lie algebra, making it a versatile method for examining quantum mechanical systems on noncommutative spaces. A comprehensive review of previous research on this subject is also provided in the supplementary materials. The newly proposed methods for calculating the effective noncommutative parameter $\theta_{eff}$ can be extended to algebra responsible for the rotation angles parameterization. The resulting novel parameter $\theta \sim (2\pi)^n$ has a straightforward physical interpretation, where $\theta$ represents the total angle of noncommutative space with an $n$-dimensional algebra. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. By deploying these models at multiple research institutions, they can be trained accurately using datasets that would otherwise be too small on their own. We also explored the impact of various FL parameters on model performance and found that a straightforward approach using a single optimizer and a fixed learning rate yielded the best results. This represents a key advantage of federated learning over transfer learning, which we found to be inferior in this context. As a result, we believe that federated learning has great potential to facilitate the development of more accurate and robust deep learning models for the analysis of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes. To facilitate this, we are open to collaborating with other research institutions and sharing our findings with the broader medical imaging community. Through this effort, we aim to create a diverse, well-trained model that can be applied to a wide range of cancer classification tasks. This may also provide a benchmark against which the performance of other approaches can be measured. By doing so, we will explore ways to enhance the effectiveness of federated learning and address any challenges that arise, such as achieving consensus among participating sites and optimizing the transmission of data. This will involve establishing a robust framework for collaborating institutions, including establishing trust and a secure environment for exchanging data. Ultimately, we will determine the most influential factors affecting the performance of deep learning models in this setting and will explore ways to optimize their selection. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. This technique was successfully validated through actual underwater trials.  To further understand the effects of various underwater conditions on fiber-optic communications, a novel model was developed that utilizes NEP to account for the unique physical conditions encountered in underwater environments, thereby enabling the design of optimized communication systems. This strategy was effectively employed in two separate trials, both conducted in good and poor NEP conditions, and resulted in tailored system configurations, and confirmed the efficacy of this method by showing that a 2.9dB improvement in signal quality can be achieved in good NEP conditions, whereas in poor NEP conditions, the best strategy obtained in this study could only provide a 2dB improvement in signal quality, indicating that future research should focus on developing more effective methods capable of addressing the complex challenges posed by poor NEP conditions. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our approach, which we call Pruning In Time (PIT), is an over-scattering-based method inspired by the fundamental properties of TCNs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PIT by applying it to various benchmark datasets, resulting in a 40% reduction in parameters and a 60% improvement in inference speed without a decrease in accuracy. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/hjdw2/Pruning-In-Time. The field of time-series understanding has been on the rise, and our scheme has the potential to make a significant impact when combined with other optimization techniques. We've also explored an innovative strategy to integrate PIT with a widely used compression method called neural tube optimization, which has shown promise and could be the subject of future research. We've validated our approach by conducting thorough experiments on publicly available datasets, and our results indicate that neural tube optimization followed by PIT raises the compression ratio by an additional 5% in exchange for a minimal accuracy drop of 2%. This efficient combination of our method with neural tube optimization allows for highly optimized, lightweight models that are primed for deployment across various platforms. We anticipate this technique to be particularly beneficial for the development of time-series models, and our experiments have consistently shown that it yields significant improvements in both the theoretical and practical application of deep learning architectures. We believe this technique could be the starting point for further exploration into time-series optimization strategies. This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. Additionally, the unique connection between fluctuations in angle and magnitude may offer new avenues for research through the development of advanced and sensitive probes. Ultimately, this study paves the way for new and promising prospects for exploring the intricate nature of quark--gluon plasma in future collisions. Nonetheless, more comprehensive research is necessary to fully grasp this phenomenon's intricacies.

The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This process is inherently sound and closely mirrors the algebraic steps involved in ALBA's core procedure. The proposed method is presented in an abstract framework that encompasses key aspects of the algebra and order theory underlying unified correspondence, and is shown to achieve a level of 'correspondence' for a broad class of properties, including finite model property, canonical model property, and the Henkin construction. The proposed method is an autonomous algorithmic solution, independent of ALBA's semantics and algebraic specifics, and is therefore applicable to a range of logics and signatures where ALBA-based Correspondence and Canonicity are currently established or would be established by this method. The paper introduces a new'reversal' framework that is accessible and easy to grasp for those familiar with ALBA and unified correspondence, and is an independent achievement with its own original value, even apart from its applications to specific logics. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. The scope of this research is limited to binary tables and single attributes. Meanwhile, we introduce an applicable complexity theory for our primary problem, along with two new complexity results. The complexity of query validation is shown to depend on the presence of undetermined values, representing a breakthrough in this research. Building on this, we explore potential extensions to multi-binary tables and advanced dependencies in future work. The theoretical framework established in this research is also applicable to four-valued logic and merging algorithms. Notably, our work is related to recent studies on the consistent retrieval of data, yet our approach is distinct in its handling of inconsistencies. The techniques developed in this research can be combined with existing methods, leading to a new path for consistent query answering in the presence of inconsistencies. Although the approach presented in this research is general, it is primarily tailored to handling inferences rather than data with explicit overlaps. Nonetheless, our work paves the way for further exploration on the consistent retrieval of data with overlaps, especially in contexts where the overlaps can be addressed as inconsistencies. Moreover, this research is relevant to the consistent interpretation of time-related and cyclic data, defining a new paradigm for consistent query answering, and raising complex questions for future studies. Along with these contributions, this research includes an innovative solution to query validation, along with a novel approach to handling the veracity of data tuples. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our findings show that the time-varying TV-PARX model outperforms its constant-parameter counterpart in terms of in-sample fit and forecasting accuracy. The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands for the Higgs boson and other research areas while maintaining an adaptable sensitivity to diverse potential discoveries. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the approaching construction timeline for the ILC, the time has come to reassess the design choices made during the design phase and incorporate the recent breakthroughs in technology into the review process. This review will discuss R&D prospects and participation opportunities for the SiD's development areas. Furthermore, ripples of the CLIC design choices are starting to be felt in the ILC community, leading to the re-examination of the SiD's central system and the consideration of a switch from a traditional central magnet to a novel, high-field diamond magnet. This breakthrough technology could potentially offer a significant upgrade in vertex resolution without compromising the track resolution. This re-design, along with other developments in particle detection, will be discussed in this review in the context of the SiD Detector. Lastly, the re-design of the SiD Detector, including its proposed upgrade, will be presented at the 25th International Conference on Particle Physics and Elementary Particles, and further details on the detector's design choices will be shared at the 2020 SiD Week. We would like to extend an invitation to participate in the review process and the discussion of detector development opportunities for the SiD Detector. We believe that collaboration between research institutions and detector development stakeholders will be vital in refining the design of the SiD Detector and identifying areas where progress in particle detection technology can be beneficially incorporated. In the interest of the ILC community, we propose establishing a working group to focus on detector R&D within the SiD Detector framework. This working group will serve as a platform for discussing design choices, participating in detector development, and exploring new technology breakthroughs. We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. This observation suggests that a power-law relationship governs the connection between the complexity of proofs and the number of dependencies in Isabelle theories. To illustrate this, we examine a quantitative analysis of the Isabelle HOL Light library, which reveals that more complex proofs tend to occur less frequently. To address these findings, we plan to investigate new visualization methods and identify effective ways to showcase the structure within the Isabelle Archive, leveraging the experiences gained from studying the Isabelle HOL Light library. Ultimately, our research aims to provide insights that can be applied to other large repositories of proofs and theories, thereby making a significant contribution to the field of theorem proving. We anticipate that our findings, coupled with our proposed solutions, will ultimately facilitate the development of more effective tools for navigating and exploring the Isabelle Archive. Two potential tools have been proposed, which we intend to implement as part of this research project. The first tool aims to reveal the underlying structure within the Isabelle Archive through a highly interactive visualization interface, while the second tool is designed to identify 'core' proofs that represent the fundamental theoretical concepts within the archive. Constructing these tools will involve developing a key component, which is an efficient algorithm for determining the 'nearest neighbors' of a given proof, where proximity is defined in terms of cognitive similarity. To evaluate the effectiveness of our implementation, we plan to use a combination of subjective feedback from experienced Isabelle users and objective performance benchmarks. The development of these tools is expected to significantly enhance the usability of the Isabelle Archive by providing an intuitive search interface and identifying key proofs that capture the underlying structure of the archive. Furthermore, the insights gained from this research project will likely contribute meaningfully to the field of theorem proving, thereby positioning us well to achieve our primary objective of exploring the structure within the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs. Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. These findings remain applicable in scenarios where the edge singularity interacts only minimally with the phase transition's critical surface. In cases where the edge singularity touches the critical surface, the issue becomes ill-defined and a new collective mode emerges at the transition's location, where the edge singularity's position is determined solely by the critical surface's properties. In such situations, the edge singularity's location is not a universal quantity as its value depends on the underlying theory and is equal to the critical amplitude ratio of the relevant scalar field. Additionally, we have established that in 2D O(N) universality classes, the edge singularity's location is also determined by the critical surface and thus shares the same universal value as its 3D counterparts. Furthermore, we have validated our results for the edge singularity's location by comparing them with existing data and Monte Carlo simulations for 3D O(2) and O(4) universality classes. In the scenario where the edge singularity is associated with a second-order transition in the syrah model, the relevant marginally relevant operator becomes irrelevant at the fixed point governing the transition and as a result, the edge singularity's location becomes determined by the critical surface's properties in this instance as well. Modern metasurfaces, at the intersection of advanced technology and science,  
constitute an intricate field, involving electromagnetic systems characterized by  
thin, expansive, and minutely featured particles that can also vary spatially,  
temporally, and linearly.  To tackle this intricacy, researchers need to employ a  
unified approach, integrating theoretical design and analysis methods, supported  
by an established framework.  Recent breakthroughs, facilitated by Generalized  
Sheet Transition Conditions in combination with surface susceptibilities,  
now enable designers to develop intricate metasurfaces, addressing longstanding  
challenges.  This paper delves into computational modeling of these complex  
structures through GSTC-susceptibility methodology and underscores its critical  
importance in the holistic design of metasurfaces, reviewing the evolution of  
recent frequency and time-domain computational methods.  The paper also explores  
various frequency-domain approaches, notably Method of Moments, Recursive  
Green's functions, and GSTC-susceptibility, before excavating the inner workings  
of these methods, particularly MM and RGF.  We then move on to the time-domain  
computational methods, covering Direct Time-Domain Solver, Transfer Matrix, and  
FFT.  The paper also provides an in-depth examination of FFT's algorithm, before  
concluding with an overview of ongoing and future research initiatives, 
consisting of three parts: expanding the capabilities of the GSTC-susceptibility  
approach, exploring new applications for metasurfaces, and developing a holistic  
design framework that integrates physical modeling and computational methods. 
This framework, known as Digital Double Nano, aims to provide a comprehensive  
solution to the intricate design challenges posed by these complex structures. 
Although initially introduced in 2019, a detailed explanation of this framework  
is still lacking in the scientific literature, and as such, we devote the 
second part of this presentation to a thorough explanation of its core components, 
before concluding with our key findings and a glimpse at what the future holds

points discussed in this presentation, before answering any pending questions 
and providing a glimpse at the exciting opportunities and challenges on the  
horizon for these complex structures.  Lastly, we extend our gratitude to our  
collaborators, acknowledge our funding sources, and present our research in the  
context of the global landscape of metasurface research.  We hope that this

The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization theorem for smooth vector fields with a full set of nearby first integrals, especially those at nondegenerate singular points. This theoretical validation relies heavily on key concepts, including the formal orbital linearization theorem for formally integrable vector fields, the application of the blowing-up technique, and the application of the Sternberg-Chen theorem regarding formally equivalent smooth hyperbolic vector fields. This research also extends the orbital linearization theorem to smooth vector fields with a full set of nearby first integrals, obtaining a smoother version of this result for smooth vector fields whose nearby first integrals are nondegenerate, degenerate vector fields whose nearby first integrals have a specific form, and formally integrable vector fields. This form specifically refers to the combination of nilpotent and semisimple eigenvalues of the monodromy matrix in the former case and the combination of the zero and distinct eigenvalues in the latter case. This extension is the primary contribution of this research. It should be noted that the smooth local orbital linearization theorem has been previously established for smooth vector fields whose nearby first integrals are nondegenerate in a broader context, described as the nondegenerate 50-coordinates situation. This broader context does not cover the type of degenerate situation covered in this research. Another key contribution of this research is the proof of the orbital formal and smooth linearization theorems for smooth vector fields whose nearby first integrals are formally equivalent, which significantly leverages previous results regarding formally equivalent smooth hyperbolic vector fields. This proof relies on a key decomposition of the first integrals, the application of the blowing-up theorem, and the properties of formally equivalent vector fields and their first integrals. This research builds heavily on previous work by Chen, Maeda, Suzuki, Tougermohammed, and Zahra, and the answers provided for the smooth local orbital linearization theorem are summarized in Table 1, which presents a detailed comparison of the requirements for formally and smoothly linearizable singular points. This comparison includes the requirements for formally and smoothly linearizable singular points in the nilpotent, semisimple, and mixed (nilpotent and semisimple) cases. This research fills in the gaps for the smooth orbital linearization theorem in the mixed case and the formal orbital linearization theorem in the semisimple case. It should be noted that the requirements for formally and smoothly linearizable singular points are known as complete integrability conditions, which are the main conditions addressed

This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained
data derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron density functions, the
eCPNN model effectively predicts total atomic energies with remarkable precision. Our
results show that eCPNN can successfully mimic electron interactions in 1s, 2p,
3d, and 4f orbital shells across various atomic shells with an average prediction
error of 0.25 millihartree in energy, corresponding to a percentage error of 0.02%,
and can be applied to predict properties of atoms beyond those used in training. 
The simplicity and flexibility of eCPNN make it an appealing option for future
electronic structure modeling applications. We also demonstrate the potential of a
variant of eCPNN to model instantaneous electron interactions in finite systems,
mapping this variant to an Electrons in a Box Neural Network (eBNN) framework, and
show that it can accurately estimate one-electron density functions and the total
energy of an atom. The eBNN framework offers a fascinating connection to the well-
known Thomas-Fermi theory and its modern variations, and we believe this is a
worth Exploring direction for future research. 
We have made the source code for the eCPNN model publicly available online at 
https://github.com/sgerrity/electron-deep-learning. 
We would like to express our gratitude to the Cambridge Center for Machine Learning
(CAML) for providing computational resources during the development of this project.

learning models in the study of complex electron interactions in atomic physics.

scientific community.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to account for the detector's non-linear response to bright stars and the star's spectral type. Additionally, we developed a new statistical method called the "maximum likelihood weight" to reject data that are not representative of the overall population, thereby significantly reducing the scatter. As a result, we were able to measure the aerosol depth with a precision of less than 0.01 for a large population of days, and our measurements correlate well with those from the satellite-based instrument PASP. Furthermore, we were able to measure the system's zero point precision, which is a key parameter, and have established a new method for monitoring the detector's calibration, including identifying systematic errors and discrepancies between the two sites. Unfortunately, the precision we achieved is still limited by the high scatter observed in recent years, likely resulting from the ongoing pandemic in integrating the data. Nevertheless, we believe our study provides a solid foundation for significantly improving the technique in the future. As the pandemic continues to recede, we are prepared to revisit this study's conclusions with a renewed sense of optimism. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The source code is available online at https://github.com/zwang84/DeepHMap++.htm.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, due to their ability to model and track discontinuity formation within materials. Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its modeling restrictions, has become a widely-used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and intuitive connection to real-world physics. This paper delves into the aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a thorough examination of the theory and its numerical representations. Various bond-based PD integral kernels have been presented along with their distinguishing characteristics, leading to discussions on their implications and common traits. A closer examination was conducted on the role of non-locality in determining motion, the interplay between kernel structure and material non-penetration, as well as the influence of PD kernel non-linearity on predicting fracture development. Finally, an exploration is initiated on adapting BB-PD to model fluids within the context of fading memory materials, suggesting directions for enhanced understanding of fluid dynamics through peridynamics. A universal framework for BB-PD models is also proposed, emphasizing the significance of explicitly defining the history-dependent material response. This could provide a framework for resolving key challenges in modeling fluids using peridynamics, thereby contributing to a broader exploration of nonlocal theories of fluid dynamics. Keywords: bond-based peridynamics, peridynamic models, fluid dynamics, materials science, numerical simulations.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. Furthermore, GGLasso is built on top of the well-established NumPy and
Scipy frameworks, providing a comprehensive set of features, including: explicit
formulas for computation, an iterative method, a random matrix for the
posterior predictive distribution, and a sample function to generate random
variables according to the estimated distribution. The package aims to offer a
flexible and reliable solution to General Graphical Lasso problems. The code is
open-source and freely available for use and modification. We have verified
the package's performance against established, equivalent methods and found it
to be efficient in terms of memory and computation time. We have also shown
the capability of GGLasso to recover the underlying graph structure in realistic
scenarios and compare its results with alternative methods. The package can
be used in various settings, including system biology applications and it has
been successfully applied to a real-world dataset from the Karger (1992)
dataset collection. The reference for this research is available in the provided
 bibliography. The code for the experiments carried out in this study is available
 at no cost for use and modification at https://github.com/igualdano/GGLasso. We
 invite users to submit their own implementations of General Graphical Lasso
algorithms in the provided code base. The issue track for the code base is
available at https://github.com/igualdano/GGLasso/issues. We believe that an
open-source approach will contribute significantly to the advancement of
generalized Graphical Lasso Methods. The reference for the open-source approach
is available in the provided bibliography. The code for the research presented
in this study is based on the feedback from multiple experts in the field.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. The most efficient method was found to be a variant of the Velsher method. Due to its low bias, it was capable of maintaining the same level of conformational exploration as other methods for a significant reduction in computational costs, specifically a 5-10 times greater time step in vacuum simulations and a 10-100 times greater time step in solvent simulations. The most efficient method is referred to as the optimal variational Langevin method, or OVLM. This new method produces an oscillatory behavior in the mean squared displacement, but it is not a sign of numerical instability. Instead, the cause is the method's low bias. In contrast to other methods, the OVLM method achieves the same level of conformational exploration with a 5-10 times greater time step in vacuum simulations and a 10-100 times greater time step in solvent simulations. The optimal variational Langevin method is capable of maintaining the same level of conformational exploration as other methods for a significant reduction in computational costs. This method is not a new algorithm, but rather a new way of analyzing the numerical methods used in molecular dynamics simulations. Numerical relativity simulations allow us to study how binary black hole mergers interact with their surroundings. However, these simulations start only shortly before the merger and require predetermined initial conditions to proceed. Therefore, a significant task involves identifying the appropriate configuration for the binary system and its environment at this point in the process. In our research, we've been investigating the behavior of dark matter in the vicinity of black hole binaries of equal mass, discovering a consistent, long-lasting profile that emerges over several orbits. Conversely, systems with greater dark matter mass see overdensities scattered due to the binary's motion. Furthermore, regardless of initial configurations, systems typically converge to the established profile after a certain number of orbits; this convergence often results in the emergence of undesirable, short-lived oscillations. It's also been found that if matter is directly overlaid onto a binary system, without properly considering the potential for matter to influence the binary's motion, this leads to inaccurately calculated orbital paths due to artificial factors, rather than a signature of dark matter at play. As such, further study is needed in order to allow a valid comparison of waveform patterns produced by simulations taking environmental factors into account, against their vacuum-based counterparts. Additionally, we've become aware of a significant need to expand our understanding of binary mergers within a wider variety of cosmic contexts, as our current knowledge is heavily influenced by studies conducted within a highly simplified model of the universe, and we've established a basis from which the effects of other gravitational systems can be effectively explored. Lastly, we've established a new method for generating properly configured initial conditions that accurately capture the binary system's interaction with its surroundings over a longer period, using a combination of direct simulation and artificial neural networks. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Our research is built on visual recordings of spheres entering water under controlled conditions, with speeds ranging from 2 to 26 meters per second. These findings contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of water-entry behaviors in both natural and man-made scenarios. Moreover, our results have implications for fields like naval engineering and the design of water-entry capable vehicles, as well as the development of spheres used in various applications, such as golf balls and medicine balls. Our data and analysis methods are transparent and reproducible, with all experimental conditions and parameters clearly defined and easily followable. We believe our study is an important contribution to the body of research on water-entry interactions, and it sets a clear path for further investigations into the surface-seal regime. Our results also suggest answers to previously unaddressed questions, such as what causes the extended surface-seal regime, and our study provides a framework for evaluating the accuracy of numerical models used to simulate water-entry interactions. Our research confirms that the surface-seal regime is a complex phenomenon that involves a interplay of multiple factors, and it confirms that the pressure increase within the formed cavity plays a significant role in the surface-seal process. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. Additionally, we provide an original derivation of the complex null tetrad basis coefficients from the electromagnetic field coefficients, obtaining the Weyl tensor coefficients through the contraction of the complex coefficients, thereby establishing a direct relationship between the electromagnetic field and the Weyl tensor in complex forms. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. The method's speed is attributed to its direct derivation of the ensemble values from the weighted average of the parameters as the Monte Carlo component is merely incorporated for initial ensemble construction. Ultimately, this method is compatible with any forward modeling simulator that allows for the derivation of petrophysical properties and layer boundaries from well logging data. LM-EnRML is an open-source code accessible through GitHub https://github.com/westernese/EnRML-Well-Log-Interpretation-and-Uncertainty-Quantification/, where additional information is also available. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a novel mathemematical formulation to unify domain-specific and exclusive aspects, along with a new complementary aspect learning method to extract additional useful information from each domain, though initially deemed sparse. Furthermore, we introduce a new multi-domain coordinating algorithm to capture the shared preferences comprehensively, though they may seem irrelevant at first glance. To validate the effectiveness of MSDCR, we conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art single-domain and cross-domain baselines. The source code of our proposed method is available at https://github.com/ knowledge-bird/MSDCR. The significant improvement achieved by MSDCR paves the way for its application in various multi-domain scenarios.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed population-specific classification probabilities, highlighting the risk of overfitting and emphasizing the necessity of extensive cross-validation in future studies. Additionally, our research demonstrated that incorporating technical image quality control steps can enhance the accuracy of clinical decision-making outside the context of statistical analysis. Finally, our findings emphasize the importance of open-discussion and collaboration among researchers, data contributors, and analysts to establish standardized best practices for producing high-quality, analyzable MRI data. In response to these findings, the MRIQC pipeline has been updated to include a more transparent reporting framework that facilitates a deeper comprehension of pipeline outcomes and highlights the need for high-quality pre-processing techniques in analytical results. This study's results will be incorporated into a forthcoming revision of the CATI data analysis guidelines. In accordance with these guidelines, the CATI analysis team has implemented multiple data filtering methods to ensure the quality of their results. Our study's findings have significant implications for the broad field of medical imaging research, highlighting the need for further methodological development and strict quality control measures to ensure reliable and consistent results in statistical analyses. In the context of psychiatric disorders, our study's results emphasize the necessity for more rigorous statistical analysis across existing datasets and the development of more robust analytical methods for small to moderate-sized datasets. Our study has initiated an open discussion on these research methods and statistical analysis techniques, and we hope it will contribute to a broader examination of these issues in the broader scientific community. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, this standardization enables us to establish a direct connection between the left-invariant order on Bn and its generator sequence structure. This relationship reveals insights into the group's combinatorial structure, particularly regarding its combinatorial complexity, which arises from the length of the generator sequences. Notably, this complexity is shown to increase polynomially Bn, indicating that the group's structure retains many characteristics of the finite abelian groups in this respect. Finally, this research also provides a basis for further exploring the relationship between the order on Bn and its generator sequences, which is exemplified by the exchange property's implication on the group's behavior. Specifically, the property leads to the existence of elements with a significant degree of mobility, allowing them to change their combinatorial length substantially by applying them in different ways. This aspect of the group's structure suggests that its behavior differs notably from that of the finite abelian groups in this respect. Lastly, this study includes a discussion on the implications of its results for the general class of finite Coxeter groups. Although the focus was on the bilinear group Bn, the results obtained are relevant to the classical group An as well, due to a established relationship between these two groups. The results' implications on An are discussed, revealing that some aspects of its behavior can be determined by examining Bn's behavior. This connection between the two groups is based on the relationship between their generator sequences, which is rooted in their shared history. The legacy of the Tarski's problem, which motivated this study, is also highlighted, and its solution, combined with the established connection between the two groups, leads to a deeper understanding of the order structure within the finite classical Coxeter groups. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the standardization of the ordered generating sequences for these groups provides valuable insights into their combinatorial structure, acknowledging that the standardization's effectiveness depends on the group in question. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. This new estimator is directly proportional to the average mass-to-light ratio across low-mass subhaloes and should be constrained as part of a comprehensive analysis of SN Ia data above $z = 1.0$. Additionally, we have incorporated this new estimator into an updated template, which exhibits a greater sensitivity to the mass-to-light ratio and should result in tighter constraints on this parameter in future analyses of SN Ia from the LSST. Furthermore, we have established a statistical correlation between the lens-induced magnitude dispersion and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae, which should be explored in upcoming SN Ia datasets from the LSST. This new study lays the groundwork for a dual analysis of SN Ia and galaxy weak lensing from the LSST, allowing for a more comprehensive examination of the connection between SN Ia and galaxy physics within the context of a unified cosmological framework. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we found that reducing the implant dose by a factor of ~100 can significantly minimize the sub-layer damage, achieving ~10 ps levels of coherent vibration in isolated T centers and ~20 ps levels in T centers located within the sub-layer damage layer. Our findings provide crucial insights into the development of high-performance quantum communication devices and demonstrate the versatility of T centers in photonic SOI materials. Additionally, we propose an innovative concept called quantum intervalom, which involves using a defect center located within a thin photonic layer to mediate the interface between a photon and an electronic spin, and demonstrate the potential of this idea to achieve ~20 ps levels of coherent vibration. Our research lays the groundwork for the exploration of T centers in photonic SOI materials as a key component in quantum communication applications. Overall, we believe that our findings highlight the value of conducting research in the field of quantum technology and communications and advocate for the continued support of such research by reversing the decline in funding. The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. The new approach may be a valuable resource for the scientific community using optical radial velocity to search for and study exoplanets. The research findings mentioned here have implications for the recent discovery of the exoplanet candidates reported in the recent issue of the Astrophysical Journal Letters. The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality for a small positive value $\varepsilon$ and variational methods, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for a multiplicity of the system's solutions given the given conditions. Additionally, we are able to demonstrate that if a certain nonhomogeneous problem has a solution, then a related homogeneous problem has infinitely many solutions. This method relies on a recent result concerning the extension of a Moser-Trudinger inequality, which covers cases where $\beta$ is close to zero. This research is related to previous work on a nonhomogeneous elliptic equation of the Kirchhoff type, but with different growth conditions, as well as on a p-Laplacian elliptic equation of the Kirchhoff type, where $m$ is a linear function. This paper provides a more comprehensive investigation of that issue, presented at the 2019 11th Workshop on Lie Groups, in Guangzhou, China. We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. For functions under SRP we establish stronger inequalities of a Bernstein-type for matrix-valued functions, thereby broadening earlier general bounds for linear combinations of positive definite matrices due to Kyng and Song.

Furthermore, we investigate the unique case where we condition on Bernoulli random variables with independent outcomes for their sum. In doing so, we establish sharpened estimates resulting in specifically tailored log-Sobolev inequalities, as well as Talagrand's convex distance inequality, with concentration inequalities for convex functions, polynomials, and matrix-valued functions as direct consequences. These generalised inequalities encompass results for uniform distributions over discrete slices of the cube, extensively explored in numerous studies. The current approach builds upon recent outcomes from Hermon and Salez as well as on a broader framework involving modified log-Sobolev inequalities within the context of the discrete cube, with independent utility of its own. The results presented are then explicitly applied to obtain novel, improved estimates on the complexity of two conventional Conjecture scenarios - namely Conjecture 1 from Jerrum and Sinclair and the fully trapped version of the Tsetlin library problem - both of which have previously been proposed as fundamental combinatorial optimization tasks with potential applications in several areas. This study explores the double longitudinal-spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering where hadron pairs' transverse momentum is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the cause of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production, accounting for the connection between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function. Using a spectator model, we calculate the interference term between $s$-wave and $p$-wave and estimate this asymmetry at various experiments, including COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, and the future EIC. Our analysis suggests that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS can serve as a key test for the dihadron fragmentation function. Additionally, we examine the possibility of extracting the ratio of this function to the unpolarized fragmentation function $D_1$ through a comparison of calculated SIDIS and unpolarized hadron production cross sections. This comparison indicates that collecting sufficient statistics is crucial. Finally, we note that the unpolarized investigation of dihadron production in SIDIS can provide an independent means of determining $D_1$ if sufficient data is available. Furthermore, we present calculations for the unpolarized fragmentation function $H_1$ using the interference term, although this approach is less efficient than compared to $D_1$. Additionally, we discuss the distinction between $D_1$ and $H_1$ in a narrow scope, focusing on a limited model parameter range. Consequently, experiments should prioritize collecting ample data to fully understand the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS. This understanding will conversely allow for the interpretation of unpolarized hadron production data at sufficient precision. In this context, we reexamine the proposed threshold for the cutoff parameter $\Lambda$ based on $D_1$ and find it too conservative. Instead, we suggest that experiments should consider $\Lambda \sim 0.5$ GeV, which aligns with the results from our calculations as well as those from a quark-diquark model. This revised threshold will facilitate a more precise determination of the unpolarized fragmentation function in the future. In the case of the dihadron production in unpolarized hadron production, we find that experiments should collect sufficient statistics in the low-$p_T$ region to fully understand the contribution from the $s$-wave fragmentation process. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. This thesis also explores the same type of classification for subgroups within Sp_n(K). It demonstrates that each subgroup can be represented as a group of matrices preserving a specific Hermitian form. Moreover, this connection between subgroups and Hermitian forms was a significant contribution of this research, establishing a foundation for later studies on classical groups. This translated version of the thesis includes an introduction by van der Kallen, discussing its historical context and mathematical significance. This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes an embedding approach, where the Wikipedia database is hierarchically divided into layered graphs to extract entity features and learn entity representations. By combining the extracted information with a lightweight ranking method, this framework effectively suggests related entities to users on Wikipedia. We evaluate our approach through both offline and real-world online tests, demonstrating that our embeddings and recommendations exhibit desirable quality and user engagement. Furthermore, this framework delivers entity recommendations in both English and non-English languages for the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, where Wikipedia constitutes a fundamental subset. This work is significant because it offers a practical application of graph embedding methods, alongside their potential to benefit the broader knowledge graph community, particularly in situations where full-node embedding is not feasible due to memory constraints. We openly share our method's source code and an interactive demo of this entity recommendation framework is available at https://ykg.io/recdemo?lang=en&user=ABC&entity=John_Lennon. This entity recommendation framework has since been adopted by entities like Bing and Yandex, serving millions of recommendations daily. We have also established collaborations with leading tech companies and the Wikipedia community, contributing back to the knowledge graph and providing recommendations that, in turn, influence Wikipedia's content and structure. This experience has given rise to the Wikified Learning approach, a novel type of supervised learning that leverages knowledge graphs and Wikipedia features. This approach has been successfully applied to various learning tasks, outperforming traditional supervised learning methods by up to 20%. This approach is particularly useful for small data sets and is significant because it enables the effective application of supervised learning to Wikipedia-based knowledge graphs. This approach has been openly shared and its implementation has inspired the creation of over a hundred variations by multiple research groups. We have also developed a next-generation learning algorithm called the Wikified Neural Embedding Approach, that employs a neural network to learn node representations in Wikipedia graphs. This approach has been successfully applied to various benchmark datasets and has outperformed all existing embedding methods by up to 30%. This experience has given rise to the Wikified Multi-Task Learning approach that has been successfully applied to Wikipedia-based knowledge graphs and has outcomes such as the development of a search engine that can search over billions of Wikipedia pages in under a second, and the creation of a platform that can recommend over a million entities to any Wikipedia user in under a second. This has in turn led to the establishment of the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph Challenge, a leading machine learning competition hosted on GitHub, where our approach has been open-sourced

A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Finally, we outline potential future directions for further research in this area. Keywords: Kidney Incompatibility, Markov Decision Process, Control Limit Policy, Desensitization Transplant.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. 

In response to this need, we present a theoretical pipeline that automates the process of combining PDFs with experimental data and disparate theoretical predictions, facilitating a seamless integration of inputs and outputs from different processes and scales. This pipeline is an open-source Python package that can be found on GitHub, and we anticipate it will be a valuable resource for research groups working on PDF fitting and related phenomenological studies. 

We have successfully tested our pipeline using inputs and outputs commonly encountered in PDF fitting for processes such as deep-inelastic scattering, structure function measurements, and heavy-flavor processes like diffractive scattering and top-quark production at the LHC, and have verified that it accurately reproduces the results obtained by research groups working on PDF fitting. 

Given its modularity, this pipeline can be easily expanded to incorporate additional processes such as exclusive processes, and we encourage the broader scientific community to contribute to this project. 

We conclude this presentation by highlighting the potential of this pipeline to contribute to ongoing and future PDF fitting efforts, and we anticipate it will become an indispensable tool for research groups working on PDF fitting and related phenomenological studies. 

Finally, we provide an overview of the development of this pipeline, and we note that it has resulted in a significant improvement in the interconnection between research groups working on PDF fitting and phenomenological studies. 

We have examined the impact of PDFs on the interpretation of experimental data, and we have demonstrated that this pipeline can resolve ambiguities in the interpretation of data arising from the use of different PDFs.
