A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Finally, our research raises the question of whether there exists an infinite family of cubic graphs exhibiting the PMH-property. Our evidence suggests no such family exists by comparing our infinite papillon family with another property - the Hamiltonian-3-edge-colouring (H3C) property, which would imply that every graph's 3-edge-colouring can be converted to a Hamiltonian cycle. Our main contribution is a sub-class of the papillon graph family that satisfies the H3C property, as well as the E2F and PMH-property, providing the first instance of a cubic graph exhibiting the PMH-property. This work is a result of our investigations into the properties of papillon graphs and their relations to perfect matchings, Hamiltonian cycles and edge-colourings. Our findings are based on local transformations, as well as applications of Tutte's Theorem and Petersen's Theorem. Our approach to studying the structure of cubic graphs through edge-colourings and matchings may also offer a new perspective on their relationship. Our research has implications on the distribution of E2F and PMH non-bipartite cubic graphs, as well as those that satisfy the H3C property, indicating that these classes share common characteristics. The universe's dark matter abundance is dictated by the Standard Model Higgs boson-mediated process, yet its interaction with nucleons via the exchange of Higgs bosons is heavily suppressed due to its pseudo-Goldstone nature. As a result, the proposed model avoids restrictions imposed by direct dark matter detection experiments. Furthermore, we pinpoint model parameter regions that replicate the observed dark matter density in accordance with the Large Hadron Collider constraints and the findings of Fermi-LAT and MAGIC in their dark matter search endeavors. The potential of future particle and astrophysical experiments to detect the proposed pseudo-Goldstone boson dark matter is also illustrated. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. In addition, our approach exhibited versatility in adapting to various game phases, and we discovered that certain situations led to suboptimal performances, suggesting areas for further improvement. To facilitate replication and exploration of future research directions, we made our data and implementation publicly available. By pushing the frontier of strategic decision-making in soccer, our work paves the way for investigating other high-performance scenarios. To share our findings with the broader soccer community, we created an interactive tool to visualize the recommended actions and compare the performance of different policies. This includes a network policy derived from our training process and other baseline policies. For instance, we found that consistently applying a standard decision-making algorithm resulted in the team shooting the ball in about 40% of situations, which aligns with the actual data from European soccer matches. In contrast, our optimized policy advised shooting in around 30% of cases, demonstrating the potential for further refinement of soccer strategies. We also explored how our approach performed under different state space coverage, finding that a higher level of coverage led to a greater difference in performance. To achieve this level of success, we realized that incorporating a critical aspect of soccer games, namely the passage of time, was essential. By acknowledging this temporal element, we could enhance the efficiency of our reinforcement learning process, cutting the required training data by nearly threefold. In response to these insights, we revised our approach to incorporate time-based sampling, exploiting the game's inherent structure to accelerate the learning rate. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. These innovations set the stage for the incorporation of time-domain data or wavefields in future extensions of the ESI method. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. To mitigate the risk of these models being superficially skilled, the paper introduces an method to combine the proposed evaluation tasks with conventional text generation metrics, resulting in a hybrid objective function that guides the model to balance its performance against these tasks while refining its performance on the original objective function through the use of a second transfer learning approach. Our results demonstrate that both proposed solutions yield models that exhibit improved performance on the evaluation tasks while maintaining their original performance in generating coherent text. This work's findings may also be applicable to other sequence-to-sequence tasks that involve generating coherent text based on prior text. In addition, the paper introduces two novel evaluation metrics that can be applied to both intramodal and intermodal dialogue understanding tasks. In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images. Experiments validate the code optimization approach, yielding a notable enhancement in reconstruction quality for both demosaicing and compressed video reconstruction. The method is made accessible through an open-source code named OptCP.

segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion.

transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations.  We also predict that 
exceptional van Hove singularities may also emerge in other pseudogapped 
metals closer to a Fermi surface with two separate components.

singularities via resonant x-ray scattering, ultrasound velocity, 
and lattice susceptibility measurements.  We conclude that the 
electron interaction's strong influence may render a typical metal

the longer-range interactions affecting the cuprate's electrically

The youth are increasingly relying on Instagram as a source of information, with political figures leveraging the platform to disseminate opinions and agendas. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on communities of co-commenters. Our analysis revealed salient co-interactions - instances of user engagement occurring more frequently than chance would suggest - to be crucial in driving online discussions and information dissemination. We based our study on 10 weeks of data surrounding key elections in Brazil and Italy, observing users who commented on posts from politicians and celebrities. We found communities centered on politics to be more active in discussions, with members producing longer comments containing more emojis, hashtags, and negative language compared to communities focusing on other topics. Additionally, we observed a diverse range of topics over time, with some topics receiving fleeting attention while others centered on fundamental issues continued to be actively discussed. Communities involved in politics displayed dynamic characteristics, with some users consistently contributing to discussions and retaining their status as top commenters. A user's influence within a community was found to be a combination of their initial reputation and the value they provide to the community in the form of interesting comments. We also noticed a significant difference between the roles of politicians and celebrities in driving online discussions and information dissemination. Finally, we verified the efficacy of our methods in replicating the findings of previous studies on social influence and community dynamics, and we found that a approach we developed, which integrates network science methods with temporal data analysis, yielded the most accurate results. Our study's findings provide insights valuable to companies seeking to monitor online discussions, track influencer activities, and assess the effectiveness of celebrity endorsements. Furthermore, our analysis offers governmental organizations a framework through which to observe online discussions, track public opinion, and evaluate the impact of political figures' actions on society. The approach we developed is equally applicable to studying discussions on other social media platforms. Our study demonstrates the value of network science in analyzing online discussions and the importance of integrated methodology that considers the unique characteristics of the platform, data, and community being studied. Additionally, we believe that our approach may be adapted to investigate the dynamics of discussions surrounding other important topics, such as sports, memes, and news. Our study showcases the effectiveness of time-series network analysis, a approach that we hope will be a valuable reference for researchers working within this field. Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization dependent on direction, and unique localized field enhancements.
A new study proposes a graphene patch structure, showing that the line waves produced can operate in the optical range.
The design involves a graphene surface integrated with an epsilon near zero substrate, which considers the effects of both dual and uniform reactive impedances.
However, this work specifically focuses on utilizing line waves in dual impedance structures. 
A finite element method simulation of the proposed design revealed line wave modes and their characteristics, and it was found that the operation frequency of line waves can be adjusted by changing the size of the patch structure.
The unique properties of line waves make them suitable for applications such as nonlinearity enhancement, localized field resonance, and steering of line waves. 
The line wave's steering capability can be achieved through a variation in its propagation distance along the boundary, and its interaction with surface plasmons. 
Overall, the line waves produced by the proposed design offer promising potential for future applications in the optical range. 
One potential application for line waves is their use a sensors, as their small size means they can detect minute changes in the surface impedance of the dual meta surface. 
The line waves produced by the proposed design also provide opportunities for line wave steering, and the localization of the line wave's field could be useful in applications such as nonlinear frequency conversion and optical phase modulation. 
However, the line wave's high loss at high frequencies may limit its effectiveness in some applications. 
Despite this challenge, the line waves produced by the proposed design could provide a useful solution to the technical hurdle of achieving high speed, low loss transmission in optical communication systems. 
The line wave's steep slope may also make it suitable for optical pulse steering, and the localization of the line wave's field could be useful in applications such as nonlinear frequency conversion and optical phase modulation. 
However, the line wave's high loss at high frequencies means that its use case will likely be in the lower frequency range of the optical window.

Although a key function in database management, query evaluation classification lacks comprehensive guidelines when dealing with self-joined queries. Our investigation aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining how self-joins impact the complexity of enumerating database results, building on existing research. By extending two known categories of classification to incorporate self-joined queries with respect to efficiency, this study provides an in-depth analysis and illustrates potential enumeration strategies using self-joins. These advancements lead to more complex proof of intractability in comparison to queries without self-joins. Additionally, this study introduces an existing method to prove intractability in the presence of self-joins and sets criteria for both feasible and infeasible queries with limited complexity, providing answers for low-arity queries and those with cyclic patterns. However, many cases remain unclear. Many expert opinions suggest that, in general, queries without self-joins can be evaluated efficiently, but this study shows that the addition of self-joins may introduce intractability even in simple scenarios. Therefore, being careful with our definitions, we are changing the first condition to ensure that, at least in theory, the added self-joins might be unnecessary. Interestingly, if these self-joins are indeed unnecessary, the classification of queries without self-joins is consistent with existing knowledge. Nevertheless, if they are necessary, our results suggest that there are many cases of intractability, contradicting a previously suggested alternative and indicating that the added self-joins do indeed matter. Furthermore, by exploring possible relationships between queries with and without self-joins, we are demonstrating that in some instances, being able to efficiently evaluate the latter implies the ability to efficiently evaluate the former. Building on these findings, we are establishing a new connection between two different categories of classification and proposing a new method for enumerating database results efficiently. This knowledge can be applied to resolve another long-standing open question. Finally, our investigation also highlights an interesting connection between two different approaches to classifying queries. With these contributions, this study provides significant insights into the complex relationship between database queries and efficiency, especially when self-joins are involved, and pinpoints many areas where further research is needed. Nonetheless, solving one of the long-standing open questions posed at the beginning of this study, we are confident that these results will be valuable for both database theory experts and those working in the field of computational logic. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. A key property of continuous functions in one direction yields a counterpart property for computable functions in another direction, and this connection enables a new way to define functions using a type of automaton that is more flexible than the usual finite-state transducers. 

On the theoretical side, this involves establishing an equivalence between different types of transducers that is driven by the proposed decision-making approach. A key aspect of the proposed solution is a new property called left-continuity for functions, and proving that continuities can be composed from combinations of left-continuous and right-continuous components.

In a recent experiment involving a highly complex system with distinct time scales and multiple coexisting patterns of behavior, a reservoir computer of the new design demonstrated several advantages over its traditional counterpart. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. The modified logic maintains the same validity properties as the original, yet its expressiveness is significantly enhanced due to the ability to leverage diverse quantification techniques, including variadic quantification. We have established the applicability of this variant to various program properties, including termination, correctness for solitary outputs, and convergence for interactively embedded programs. We have further introduced a novel application to the verification of programs with dependence on multiple references. Finally, we have outlined a future direction for integrating the proposed logic with program linearization. The original proposal by Unruh in POPL 2019 was a key inspiration for the present work.

We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ due to previous work by Hildebrand and Saias. Without making any assumptions, we derive a more general formula that gives the count of y-friable integers for the larger range of $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. This formula reveals a pattern that follows $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ times correction factors. The correction factors consider the influences of zeta zeros and prime powers. By having this more general formula, we resolve two long-standing conjectures of Hildebrand and Pomerance. 

Hildebrand initially hypothesized that once $y$ is smaller than $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, the count of y-friable integers would no longer follow the estimated $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ pattern, which we confirm to be true.

Since we now have a more general formula, we can see that under optimal conditions, and once $y$ is smaller than $(1+\varepsilon)\log x$, this difference indeed falls below $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$.

The Euclid satellite, set to launch in 2022, will significantly influence future cosmological research with its Visible and Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer instruments. The authors of this study analyzed how correlated readout noise affects in-flight measurements for the NISP detectors and proposed an analytical method for noise covariance matrices. Through experimental data analysis, a 1/f-like noise model was fitted to the NISP engineering detectors and their noise characteristics were determined, allowing for more accurate flux measurements via maximum likelihood estimation. It was found that using this approach, a four-fold decrease in measurement bias compared to the white noise model was possible. The authors conclude that even with the white noise model, negligible bias on NISP's in-flight measurements will be maintained, meeting Euclid's processing baseline requirements. The proposed 1/f-like noise model, however, is expected to yield even more substantial gains in terms of precision. The authors suggest that this new model should be adopted for the NISP data processing pipeline. The impact of the adopted processing strategy on in-flight measurements was examined and it was found that, although slightly impaired by the higher noise model, the NISP's in-flight performance will still closely match the satellite's baseline expectations. The implications of using the 1/f-like noise model for NISP data, including a small bias correction, are discussed and the results presented. The authors conclude that the adopted processing strategy will allow for in-flight measurements that are in line with Euclid's baseline requirements and the implications of the model will be taken into consideration for the final in-flight configuration of the NISP instrument. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our study provides insights into the dynamics of rumor propagation and influential measurement, as well as effective prediction techniques, that can be applied to other epidemic phenomena. Additionally, we developed and released an open-source repository containing our implementation details and statistical data. With the increasing diffusion of COVID-19 influenced online rumors, our research is timely and relevant, with implications for the development of advanced prediction models. Furthermore, our study is an important contribution to the field of computer ethics, addressing critical issues related to the prevention of information disorder. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. This significant breakthrough in determining galaxy distances relies heavily on wide-field observations covering the central regions of galaxies. Furthermore, a significant correlation was discovered between the measured distances to galaxies and the previously estimated distances to the galaxies within the Fornax cluster when using another method, and distinct population patterns were found within the Fornax cluster. Moreover, a comprehensive study was conducted of the relationship between the measured distances to galaxies and their core velocity dispersions, as well as a comprehensive analysis of the population patterns of the galaxies within the Fornax cluster. The comprehensive database of the planetary nebulae sources within the Fornax cluster provides significant scientific value for future studies of the galaxies within the Fornax cluster. Additionally, a comprehensive discussion was held on the most suitable methods for detecting the planetary nebulae sources within the galaxies within the Fornax cluster and the most suitable criteria for differentiating the genuine planetary nebulae sources from the false positives. This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. A mathematical proof is provided to show that a timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve in a four-dimensional Euclidean space is actually a straight line. An alternative approach, using a different method of classification, is also established to demonstrate that a curve in a higher dimensional Euclidean space can be either a straight line, a circle, or a curve classified as a planar Bertrand curve when classified alternately. This concept is expanded to include a new category of curves, called the timelike (n-1,n)-Bertrand curve, and a proof is provided to show that a timelike (n-1,n)-Bertrand curve in an n-dimensional Euclidean space is a straight line. Finally, a new definition is provided for periodically alternating curves, or curves that alternate between types, and a proof is provided to show that a curve of this type can either be a straight line, a circle, or a curve classified as a planar Bertrand curve when classified alternately. This research expands our current understanding of timelike Bertrand curves in higher dimensional space. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. We introduce a novel, adaptive strategy that dynamically evaluates and compares loss functions, paving the way for future investigations into the interplay between loss functions and neural networks. Our research is freely available as an open-source repository, encompassing both theoretical and practical aspects of loss function analysis. We anticipate our explorations to contribute significantly to the ongoing discussion on loss function research. We also introduce three compelling reasons that loss functions should be viewed as parameters rather than fixed constants, supported by concrete examples from the field of computer vision. We further explore four distinct types of loss functions, detailing their underlying characteristics and explaining how they relate to the cross-entropy method. We investigate eight diverse loss function architectures, including both commonly employed methods and novel innovations. We experiment with five distinct evaluation metrics, along with two critical performance indicators, and showcase our results across three public datasets, along with additional, previously unseen data. Our results demonstrate notable improvements over baseline performance, achieving up to a 6.51% improvement in accuracy on the CIFAR-100 dataset. We also introduce an influential factor that significantly impacts performance, identifying a key parameter that significantly affects outcome. We explore a crucial aspect that every new loss function candidate must adhere to, ensuring compatibility with the optimization process. We establish a new benchmark that surpasses state-of-the-art benchmarks on two renowned datasets, detailing our approach to optimizing the proposed loss function. We experiment with multiple ways to integrate the proposed loss function, highlighting the benefits of our approach. We provide a comprehensive overview of our method, detailing a crucial step that enables successful implementation. A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation. By leveraging a resolvent estimate for the linearized equations, we establish the stability of this feedback control approach. Key factors influencing stability include the resolvent operator's convergence and the tilting angle of the boundary orientation. We also examine how the boundary orientation impacts stability through numerical studies. Additionally, a state observer for the nonlinear Navier-Stokes equations is constructed using a standard Luenberger scheme, and its stability properties are established. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of both the feedback controller and state observer through numerical experiments. This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. This model's potential utility is demonstrated through its application to actual polymer materials. Furthermore, we investigate the effect of drawing-induced orientation on material behavior and observe unique anisotropic properties in drawn polymers. Additionally, we examine the model's capability to model materials with previously formed crystalline regions. This model contributes to the broader development of theory on strain-induced crystallization and its impact on polymer thermomechanical behavior. It paves the way for further experimental and numerical studies on the unique properties of polymers that undergo drawing-induced crystallization. It is also essential for the design of engineering components made from polymers with previously formed crystalline regions. This model is an important step in the extension of its 2021 counterpart. It overcomes previous limitations by incorporating essential features of polymer crystallization and obviates the necessity for crystallization models often employed in industrial applications. Those models typically rely on strongly adiabatic entropy inequality and induce unauthorized dissipation measures, thereby compromising the consistency of the model with the second law of thermodynamics. In contrast, the model's recent revision is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics and provides a more accurate representation of thermomechanical behavior in polymers. It eliminates the model's previous reliance on approximation that leads to strong adiabatic inequality and instead, uses a more precise representation of temperature evolution. This model's temperature evolution model is a stronger formulation than its predecessor. It formulates temperature evolution as a state variable change rather than an inequality. This revision ensures that temperature evolution depends on total entropy balance rather than irreversible part. One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time a state-dependent and robust online learning algorithm is applied to a real robotic experiment. Our code is available at https://github.com/vayda/CFMA. For a more detailed discussion on our results, please refer to Table 1 and Figure 1 in the paper. To summarize, our innovative approach resolves the key challenge of learning from diverse forms of corrective feedback in robotics. To learn from such domains, we can utilize our variety-seeking meta-algorithm. By doing so, we can successfully solve a critical problem affecting a broad range of learning tasks. Moreover, our results provide a significant breakthrough in addressing a critical issue in learning. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. A comparative analysis of various detection methods, including coherent and differential detection methods, is also provided, revealing that 8-ARY CPM with a 4-symbol delay in conventional differential detection holds a middle ground between these detection methods, outperforming binary PSK with a 4-symbol delay coherent detection method. Initially calculated using correlators of quantum field stress-energy tensors, the issue will now be re-examined using quantum thermodynamics. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model involves bidirectional translation of disentangled images in two directions: the translation of real rain images into clear backgrounds, coupled with synthetic rain images.  Moreover, enforcing a strategy that decomposes rain images into clear backgrounds and rain elements aids the translation of these components.  This method is further enhanced with the inclusion of disentanglement strategy using losses like cycle consistency loss and adversarial loss for both real and synthetic rain images.  A complementary entanglement strategy that is symmetrically applied is also included to aid rain simulation.  Comprehensive experiments conducted on datasets of artificial and actual rainy conditions demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other competing techniques.  Additionally, the model's capability to simulate complex real rain scenes has been validated through a subjective evaluation by multiple human observers.  The model's code has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/wh1574356/disentangled-rain-simulation-and-removal.  The model's capability to simulate real rain scenes has also been further validated through an open-access challenge hosted on the MMEditing website at https://mmediting.github.io/rain-simulation-challenge/.  The outstanding performance of the proposed model in both artificial and actual rainy condition datasets has been consistently confirmed by the top-performing models submitted to the challenge.  Notably, the proposed model has also achieved the lowest subjective evaluation score compared to all other top-performing models submitted.  The model has been found to produce rain simulations with an accuracy of 93.75 percent as verified by human observers, out of 1250 randomly selected images from the real rain test dataset.  The model's code has been written in Python using the PyTorch framework.  The proposed model has been found to experience rain-specific mode collapse and a significant increase in mode collapse in low-light conditions.  Several possible remedies for these issues have been discussed.  The paper has been submitted to the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2020.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Our approach demonstrates a notable increase in learning efficiency, with speed-ups of over 5 times, indicating the promise of our method for scaling comparative feedback-based reward learning. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ghulghule/VisCRFRL. Additionally, we've introduced a new evaluation protocol for comparative feedback-based reward learning, which emphasizes practical considerations and ORL-like scenarios, and have made this protocol available as well. It highlights the importance of modest comparison sets and suggests that simple baseline agents often outperform state-of-the-art methods when given little human feedback. Nonetheless, our results show that our VisCRFRL approach consistently achieves better performance than baseline methods, even under more challenging conditions. Evaluating a person's risk of drug abuse is crucial, and online surveys have proven effective for gathering relevant data. The data collection process included a comprehensive range of characteristics, including personality traits, impulsivity levels, and sensation seeking tendencies. The data set analyzed substance consumption patterns for 18 different central nervous system-altering substances. The research revealed that certain substances are frequently consumed in clusters, characterized by strong correlations, known as "pleiades." Notable clusters were identified around the substances ecstasy, heroin, and benzodiazepines. By exploring various classification techniques and features, a data-driven approach identified the most effective methods to categorize individuals as users or non-users for each specific substance or cluster. Among the techniques examined, including tree models and probability estimations, a top-performing classifier was chosen for each drug. The accuracy of these classifications exceeded 70 percent for nearly all substances when using a rigorous evaluation method. The best performance was seen for the substances cannabis, crack, ecstasy, legal highs, LSD, and volatile substance abuse, achieving a high classification accuracy of above 75 percent. A key factor influencing this classification accuracy was the personality trait known as "openness," followed by neuroticism and conscientiousness. Notably, certain personality traits exhibited an interesting relationship with the classification accuracy, where a more complex personality structure was associated with a higher level of correct classification. This relationship between personality traits and classification accuracy held consistent across the cluster of substances known as "classic." In contrast, the accuracy for the "modern" substances, such as legal highs and volatile substance abuse, was lower and showed a different personality trait pattern. Furthermore, a comparison with existing studies on impulsivity and sensation seeking revealed that these features alone were insufficient to achieve this level of accuracy in classification. A comprehensive evaluation of the methodology's reliability and feasibility was also conducted, incorporating a diverse range of researchers and a systematic approach to minimize bias. This involved multiple iterations of independent data sets, independent feature selection, and a fair comparison with existing studies on impulsivity and sensation seeking. The established model demonstrated excellent performance on an independent data set and a robust feature set selected through a data-driven approach. This research provides a groundbreaking model for evaluating the risk of drug consumption, surpassing the limitations of previous studies relying on simplified scenarios and lacking diversity. The data analysis revealed a high degree of differentiation among users of different substances, reflecting a complex picture of drug consumption patterns. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This resource includes detailed information on nearly 700 everyday inference patterns and approximately 160 categories of topics relevant to these patterns.  We believe that leveraging such patterns can significantly improve the performance of complex tasks such as conversational dialogue and predictive storytelling.  To test this hypothesis, we design a set of rigorous evaluation tasks including both narrow and broad scopes of reference and establish a baseline model that achieves impressive results by limiting the scope of its predictions.  However, when the scope is widened, the model's performance declines substantially, indicating a major opportunity for advancement in this area.  To build upon this foundation, we introduce an advanced model that surpasses the baseline in all metrics but still falls short of the optimal results indicated by human evaluation, suggesting a direction for future research to fully realize the potential of ATOMIC.  Our code and the full dataset are available for download at http://github.com/ygkit/atomic and http://github.com/ygkit/atomic-release, respectively.  We anticipate this resource to play a pivotal role in developing more sophisticated, human-like artificial intelligence capable of complex if-then reasoning tasks. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. Notably, our method demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art deep learning models in challenging situations involving out-of-distribution data. Furthermore, clinical practitioners have evaluated the reconstructed images for clinical usability, confirming the good performance of our method. We believe this novel, physics-informed deep learning approach can serve as a platform for exploring innovative solutions to other low-dose imaging problems. We have made our model publicly available for others to use. High-resolution reconstructions and additional information about this work can be found on our website. We have also outlined potential research directions for further development of this model, and we hope this will inspire others to contribute to related projects. We have incorporated feedback from multiple practitioners and researchers in the field of PET-MRI, including those who have generously provided us with their insights on enhancing this work. We have used this feedback to revise our protocol for evaluating the clinical usability of reconstructed images, and we have modified our protocol to make it more robust to variations in imaging protocols. We have shared our revised protocol, along with our model and data, with the broader PET-MRI community. We have also established connections with leading research groups in the field of PET-MRI, and we have collaborated with multiple practitioners to ensure that our approach meets the requirements and standards of clinical practices. We have provided a detailed analysis of our method's performance in comparison to state-of-the-art models, and we have provided a comprehensive overview of our model's capabilities in the appendix. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. For nearly 60 years, researchers have been searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through SETI initiatives, with a Dyson Sphere as a primary target - an advanced megastructure capable of harnessing a star's energy for an advanced civilization. A study explores whether constructing such a structure around a black hole would be feasible and efficient in powering a civilization. Considering six potential energy sources, researchers found that an accretion disk, which can produce $10^{5}\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$ of energy, would be sufficient for an advanced civilization. Additionally, a Dyson Sphere could potentially collect energy from relativistic jets and increase its overall energy output fivefold. Calculations indicate that a Dyson Sphere constructed around a stellar-mass black hole in the Milky Way could be detectable with current telescopes using waste heat radiation in the ultraviolet to mid-infrared spectrum. Analyzing spectral energy distributions and radial velocity variations could aid in identifying possible artificial structures, such as Dyson Spheres. With about 500 billion galaxies potentially hosting suitable stars for natural variability, researchers believe that a Dyson Sphere construction project would result in only a small reduction in the variability period and amplitude compared to natural variability. Consequently, the detection of such a phenomenon would have significant implications. Additionally, detecting a Dyson Sphere would offer a means to derive the civilization's energy needs and potentially shed light on its technological advancements. Furthermore, this study suggests looking for signs of energy production through nuclear reactions in the ultraviolet to mid-infrared spectrum and considers two candidates, DS And and KIC 5483470, which exhibit radio signals similar to those generated by an artificial structure. Researchers propose calling a detected Dyson Sphere "DS Radio" and suggest searching for radio communications between Earth and a Dyson Sphere. This study provides theoretical frameworks for identifying possible artificial structures, such as Dyson Spheres, and predicts the consequences of their construction. With the advent of advanced astronomical facilities such as PLATO, TESS, and the CHAI voice-assisted telescope, researchers are confident that they will be able to detect a Dyson Sphere in the near future. In the event of a discovery, the community faces a significant ethical dilemma - whether to establish communication with the civilization or maintain secrecy. This study contributes a framework for addressing this dilemma by suggesting that, in the event of a detection, the scientific community should first verify the findings through a consensus approach before publicly disclosing the information and considering communication options with the civilization. Network-based services provide significant income to service operators, which they regulate through agreements on performance. Ensuring these agreements are being met necessitates the monitoring of service standards. A method to accomplish this involves deploying active measurement tools, which send test traffic and gauge performance. Nonetheless, these tools demand substantial resources and often fail to cover the whole network. Human administrators decide what parts to measure, which proves inefficient and unresponsive to rapidly changing network conditions. This article discusses the advantages of employing peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to enhance the identification of SLA breaches. Initially, we explore the principles of steering active measurement tools via P2P. These principles involve autonomous decision-making across a network via a self-regulating system. Subsequently, we outline strategies for activating measurement sessions that are based on these principles, which do not need human input, can adapt to alterations in network conditions, and operate independently of underlying active measurement technologies. Finally, we examine the potential benefits, as well as several research challenges, associated with integrating P2P principles into active measurement systems. Nonetheless, integrating P2P principles into active measurement systems remains an area of extensive scientific inquiry. Two approaches can activate measurement sessions based on P2P principles: 1) using a separate system for session activation, which is decentralized and relies on human input for validation, or 2) using a centralized system for session activation, which is human-administered and relies on human input for validation. We propose a novel approach, 3.P2PSA, that utilizes a semi-decentralized approach for session activation based on P2P principles, incorporating elements from both previous strategies. 3.P2PSA utilizes a combination of human and automated input to set performance targets and prioritize measurement sessions, which is effective in identifying SLA breaches, managing system resources, and making decisions on session activation. The advantages of this method include the ability to respond to changing network conditions, reduce the need for human input, and minimize the risk of false positives in identifying SLA breaches. Although 3.P2PSA presents several research difficulties, it exhibits considerable potential in solving several challenges related to the detection of SLA breaches. Nonetheless, several issues related to the detection of SLA breaches, which is the identification of performance targets and prioritizing measurement sessions, remain unclear with 3.P2PSA. To address these concerns, we examine three approaches for defining performance targets: static, dynamic, and collaborative, as well as three approaches for prioritizing measurement sessions: random, proactive, and reactive

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. To validate these findings, a start-of-art energy recovery linac currently under development in Korea is used as an example, with numerical simulations showing that its beam breakup threshold could be as low as 25 mA if design improvements are implemented. The paper also presents several practical suggestions for mitigating beam breakup in multi-pass energy recovery linacs, including changing the beam fill pattern or incorporating a beam transfer matrix into the threshold current analysis to account for machine-specific dependencies. These strategies can be applied to various energy recovery linac designs facing beam breakup constraints. Ultimately, this research emphasizes the value of detailed numerical modeling in optimizing multi-pass energy recovery linac design for maximum performance. The modeled beam-RF interaction can also be applied to different types of accelerators, such as radiofrequency accelerators and specialized devices like a 79.5 MHz radiofrequency test stand currently in development in Japan. The paper's findings are relevant to large-scale energy recovery linacs such as the Future Circular Collider (FCC), where beam breakup instability above the machine's 220 mA threshold current might be induced by a 50 GeV, 2 A beam. However, it's worth noting that even if beam breakup above the design current is accounted for, it's not the limiting factor for achieving the FCC's high beam current in this specific scenario. The model's insights can also be applied to the Diamond Light Source II, a proposed storage ring that might benefit from design improvements that could enhance its threshold current. The paper concludes by highlighting the opportunities for further research in modeling beam-RF interaction and beam breakup instability in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. The development of new beam diagnostics and the associated development of modeling codes that incorporate filling pattern dependencies could contribute significantly to advancing the field. The intricacy of these models is significant, partly because existing detectors have been incapable of observing final state neutrons, which has led to significant systematic uncertainties. The implementation of 3D scintillator tracking technology in next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments has improved detection capabilities by enabling event-by-event measurement of neutron kinetic energy resulting from neutrino interactions, thus providing valuable information for refining neutrino interaction models and reconstructing neutrino energies. Prototypes of these detectors have undergone neutron irradiation at the LANL beamline in both 2019 and 2020. The primary goal was to demonstrate the ability of neutron detection by comparing the total cross-sectional area of neutrons and scintillator interaction at 98-688 MeV, which was measured at 0.36±0.05 barn, in accordance with established external measurement standards. This measurement demonstrates the capability of these detectors to enhance the accuracy of neutrino interaction models used in future long-baseline neutrino experiments. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of ongoing development in 3D neutron detection technology. In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces change in response to temperature among particles made of chondritic materials, which indicate that their surface energy drops by approximately 5 times when temperatures rise. In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effect of surface moisture on the grains under normal lab conditions, which involves having multiple water layers. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs as dust moves inward, we decided to examine how two alternative methods for dust preparation affect tensile strength, which involved letting the grains dry in the air (resulting in dry samples) or baking them into airless environments (yielding super-dry samples) as an attempt to mimic how things might appear in the cooler sections of the protoplanetary discs. In all experiments where temperatures didn't exceed 1000 K, we discovered that dry samples displayed increased sticking by approximately 10 times over their water-soaked counterparts. In temperatures of up to 900 K, super-dry samples behave identically to dry samples. Nevertheless, sticking forces in the super-dry samples shoot up to yet another increase of about 100 times in temperatures of about 1200 K. These findings imply that aggregate growth accelerates in a narrow high-temperature range, which may be a critical'sweet spot' for planetary growth. In the case of lunar formation, this could explain why the Moon ended up being so much less massive than expected. In the case of planetary systems formed in association with a stellar binary, this effect may result in planets being generated in the space between the two stars due to their unique temperature properties. In the case of small particles, the presence of water has a contrary effect, turning them into aggregates at both low and high temperatures. In the case of the larger aggregates, water appears to have the opposite effect, causing them to break apart in both low and high temperatures. In the case of water-rich planets forming in the cooler sections of the protoplanetary discs, this could result in the generation of large amounts of small particles, which in turn could produce the distinctive features seen in water-rich asteroids such as the Karuma asteroid. In the case of planets forming in the warmer sections of the protoplanetary discs, this could result in the generation of large amounts of aggregate dust, which in turn could produce the distinctive features seen in chondritic asteroids such as the Benito asteroid. Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies like Kernel Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Semi-Supervised Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis. The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggfortify in ggplot2) graphical tools. Moreover, it provides a sample dataset (OrientalDatabase) to illustrate the ease of projecting it using LFDA. The package is available on CRAN and can be installed through the regular channel. The package GitHub repository is located at <https://github/lfda>. Key functions in the package include the LFDA (lfda) and KLFDA (klfda) algorithms, data sets (OrientalDatabase and Irish) and a visualization utility (lfda3d). Orthogonal non-negative matrix factorization (ONNMF) is another crucial aspect of the package, and a discussion on its mathematical representation is provided in the LFDA R package documentation. The Irish dataset, obtained from the UCI Repository, is another dataset available within the package. The Irish dataset comprises three attribute sets, addressed as follows: (1) publicly accessible attributes (irish$Irish1), (2) hidden or pseudo attributes (irish$Irish2), and (3) combination of both (irish$Irish3). The package has been designed to facilitate an interactive SSLFDA approach, where a user interface is created utilizing Shiny. This interface allows a user to input a data matrix and the number of desired latent variables, and then executes an interactive ONNMF implementation. The result visualization is carried out through a 3D plot. The shinyUI, shinyServer, and shinyOptions functions are employed to create this interface. The package glossy available on CRAN has been utilized to create the user interface. Additionally, the package includes a demonstration of an interactive KLFDA approach. The user interface for this demonstration is created utilizing the Shiny framework. The kernel matrix is constructed using the KLFDA utility function provided in the package. This utility function employs the diagonal matrix weighting method. The 3D visualization of the KLFDA result is carried out through the rgl package. System specifications for the package development are detailed in the documentation. The package installation requirements are R (version 3.5) and the necessary utility functions

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. The source code for our framework is available online at the specified URL. EKMP outperforms the existing state-of-the-art kernelized imitation learning method by a significant margin of 45.05 seconds, or roughly 30%, in our experiments. Furthermore, EKMP achieves comparable performance to optimized motion planning methods for our evaluation tasks. EKMP's improved performance is expected to contribute positively to the development of future advanced kernelized learning algorithms. Additionally, we explored the scope for expanding our model to handle soft constraints, which indicates a potential path for future enhancements. In line with the objective of enhancing kernelized learning algorithms, we have made our model's code available for reference. In the context of motion planning, our work indicates that forming relationships between our constraints and state-of-the-art motion planning methods will be crucial for any future advancements. In the field of kernelized learning, our research has introduced a novel formula for predicting target points, which may serve as a starting point for future developments. In the domain of motion planning for robotic arms, our results have demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in achieving complex nonlinear constraints, which will likely become a standard requirement due to the ever-increasing precision of robotic sensors. To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. This work provides the foundation for further investigation of whether six-gluon amplitude properties may be understood through the application of conformal symmetry in N=4 SYM theory. In line with this, the track of a conformally invariant cross ratio was proposed, though further research is required to fully establish its significance. The results presented in this work have also implications for further BFKL developments, including potential contributions from heavier color exchanges that could be incorporated through the extension of CEV concepts. As a result of this study, explicit NNLL BFKL equations precision targets, specifically the dispersion relations for six-gluon amplitude configurations in N=4 SYM theory, have been defined. In line with these findings, the introduction of a six-gluon impact factor component in the equation of motion approach has been proposed, along with a question being raised whether a similar extension may be relevant in the context of octa-BFKL developments. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface. Lastly, we investigate the critical parameters necessary for realizing this phenomenon in the presence of Zeeman field and Rashba coupling. Our results may be relevant to guiding future research into Rashba Hubbard models within graphene and other Rashba systems with attractive interactions. Additionally, we provide an outline for potential experimental verification of our predictions via transport and heat capacity measurements in the absence of a Zeeman field. Finally, we offer potential solutions to overcome two main obstacles in the experimental realization of these results: the challenge of incorporating a Monte Carlo method and the need for more precise measurements of Rashba parameters in actual materials. Nonetheless, we believe that our findings will contribute meaningfully to the ongoing discussion on superconductivity in Rashba systems and may inspire further theoretical and experimental investigation. Additionally, we hope that our results will become a foundation for future research on the interplay between spin-orbit coupling, Zeeman field, and superconductivity in the Rashba Hubbard model. In the case of actual materials, we hope that our predictions will be validated by experimental measurement, and we anticipate that further discussion surrounding our analysis of the effects of Rashba coupling and Zeeman field will fuel the exploration of more complex models involving spin-orbit coupling. On the method side, we hope that our results will demonstrate the capability of the quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation to accurately predict the spatial distribution of Rashba paramagnets.
