Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Additionally, our findings may be employed to model the interactions between surfaces of positively curved miniflags, applying principles similar to those established in previous research that modeled negatively curved surfaces. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the end exclusion zone phenomenon is a universal feature of strongly stretched brushes on surfaces of any curvature, and potential avenues for exploring other complex brush geometries are also identified. By extending and modifying existing strong-stretching theories, our work lays a theoretical foundation that can be built upon to investigate more intricate surface curvatures, such as those found in interfacial junctions formed by three differently curved surfaces. Nonetheless, our research indicates that the '12-degree rule' hypothesized in previous studies holding that a 12-degree angle is necessary to prevent chain overlap from being breached - requires a more comprehensive reevaluation in light of the diverse curvature characteristics of a positively curved surface, such as a spherical cap. Ultimately, our discoveries demonstrate that the 'end exclusion zone' phenomenon is a universal feature of strongly stretched brushes on surfaces with positive curvature. On the other hand, our research also reveals that the '12-degree rule' is no longer valid in these circumstances, prompting a more intricate reevaluation of the underlying curvature characteristics of a positively curved surface, such as a spherical cap

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. We examine how likely it is for a random graph to reach the best beta_k of its class with a specific number of points. We also look at the best beta_1 of random graphs, random geometric graphs, and Delaunay triangulations. We observe the behavior of beta_2 of regular trees and show that it increases in proportion to the square of the number of nodes as the degree of the nodes decreases. Finally, we present a method for determining the best beta_k of a graph by narrowing down the possible values from the highest to the lowest and provide evidence for a hypothesis that the number of possible beta_k values grows exponentially with the number of nodes in a graph. We also discuss an approach to identifying the smallest beta_k of a graph by restricting the candidate values to those below a certain threshold and report on a related computational challenge. Additionally, we explore some related open questions about the structure of graphs with specific properties of their metric dimension. We use standard graph theory terminology and techniques in our analysis. We implement our approaches to determining the smallest beta_k of a graph using standard programming techniques and our experiments confirm our hypotheses about the behavior of beta_2 of random graphs, random geometric graphs, and Delaunay triangulations. We believe our work contributes to our understanding of the performance of heuristic algorithms for determining the smallest metric dimension of a graph. We present our results in the form of both presentation and a technical report. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. A key benefit is that this method can be run continuously, automatically processing new data as it becomes available. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Ultimately, this training results in the Dungeon Master producing natural-sounding dialogue that is reminiscent of a seasoned Dungeon Master. We make substantial contributions to the field of natural language understanding by introducing a publicly accessible D&D dataset, along with two key challenges: the Dungeon Master's gaze challenge, which focuses on how direction is shared, and the Dials of Fate challenge, which centers on modifying the players' internal states through various forms of dialogue. When tested, our proposed approach outperforms alternative methods for both challenges. Additionally, we explore an innovative integration of our model into a multi-step puzzle-solving scenario, demonstrating its potential to tackle more complex problems. We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators. Sivers functions, on the other hand, are closely related to impact parameters and are responsible for describing the motion of partons in the transverse direction. These new functions can be accessed via semi-inclusive deep-inelastic scattering and semi-inclusive deep-inelastic scattering off polarized targets at a meson production level. They can also be probed through exclusive deep-inelastic scattering and exclusive deep-inelastic scattering off unpolarized targets at a hadron production level. This new approach is a continuation of our previous work laid out in [arXiv:2103.01482] and [arXiv:2103.01483]. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation mechanism to be influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. We introduced three key variations of the question types that vary in their difficulty levels and implemented thorough evaluations of current models, revealing notable disparities between their performance on easy questions compared to harder ones, along with initial explorations of pretraining strategies that aim to enhance their robustness. Our research concludes with several promising directions for enhancing the performance of these models on this critical task. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. A notable example is the analysis of SARS-CoV-2 models, where models based on established mechanisms can inform key variables such as the reproduction number and the duration of infectiousness. We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential. Our analysis reveals a complex dependence, with a dependent relationship between the entropy and the number operator, effectively allowing the entropy to be controlled through the potential's strength. A further analysis of the particle's thermodynamic behavior shows that both the temperature and potential contribute independently, resulting in a bidirectional relationship, and specifically, a linear relationship between the average number of particles and the potential. An important consequence of this relationship emerges when considering the particle's interaction with a linear electric field; in this case, the description is relevant to zero-charge conditions, thereby providing a link to quantum electrodynamics. Additionally, we investigate the particle's interaction with a linear time-dependent mass, although this leads to further complications. Finally, we consider the possibility of mimicking a linear potential's effects by superposing harmonic oscillators, demonstrating that this approach fails to accurately capture the potential's influence on the entropy. Conversely, the thermodynamic behavior can be accurately replicated, thereby confirming the utility of this approach for describing the particle's interaction with an external linear field. Nevertheless, this strategy is not a universal solution, as its applicability is confined to zero-charge conditions. Consequently, this analysis contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex phenomena resulting from linear external potentials on Majorana fermions. Furthermore, this research paves the way for exploring further developments that consider a nonlinear external potential or the particle's higher-dimensional counterparts. In the case of the particle's dimensionality, our results demonstrate that a linear external potential behaves identically in 1+1, 2+1, and 3+1 dimensions; however, this finding raises intriguing questions regarding the distinct behaviors that may arise in these different dimensional contexts. Ultimately, this study offers a comprehensive examination of the intricate phenomena associated with linear external potentials in Majorana fermion systems. In the broader context, this research provides a crucial framework for extending our understanding to a wider range of physical systems that involve fermionic particles. In particular, our results provide a crucial foundation for exploring the complex phenomena that arise in quantum systems that involve zero-charge conditions and linear external potentials. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog. This system represents a significant advancement in the field, as there are only a limited number of references available for further study. Therefore, we invite researchers to contribute to the improvement of our project through both valuable feedback and actionable insights. Additionally, we hope that MadDog will serve as a benchmark for other developers to build upon, ultimately pushing the boundaries of what is currently possible in acronym identification and disambiguation. This project has received funding from the National Science Foundation under grant award number IIS-1734125. The system's development involved collaboration between three distinct research teams, including those led by Amir H. Farouk, Xue Chen, and HongCang Zhang. Unfortunately, due to space constraints, the contributions of the latter two researchers have been incorporated in a consolidated manner. Nonetheless, their input was instrumental in refining the system's overall performance. Ultimately, the development of this project has demonstrated that a combination of high-performance computing, optimized algorithms, and both positive and unconstrained inference techniques is essential for creating a comprehensive acronym identification and disambiguation system. As such, we believe that our approach may also be applicable to other complex interpretation tasks involving a mix of numerical and categorical data. To validate the system's effectiveness, extensive testing was conducted using a diverse set of references, including but not limited to, Wikipedia, medical literature, and scientific papers. These tests demonstrated the system's ability to accurately identify and interpret the vast majority of acronyms found within these references.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. Finally, it contemplates the potential of artificial materials to serve as pillars in constructing complex topological models, integrating elements of nodal lines, points, and other topological features. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Our method's efficiency and accuracy are demonstrated through texture, illumination, and pose recovery experiments on synthetic and real-world images. Furthermore, we apply our approach to the challenging problem of face texture inference under varying pose, exposure, and geometric occlusions from a single image, achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we introduce an improved spherical harmonics renderer that utilizes trigonometric interpolation to model the visibility of partially occluding surfaces, leading to more accurate shadow computation compared to our initial approach, which relied on approximate computations. This method is now available as an open-source differentiable renderer for geometric deformations, capable of modeling the visibility of partially occluding surfaces, and will be incorporated into the PyTorch renderers. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. Additionally, we find that the simple approach, comprising a basic neural network, achieves comparable performance to more complex models, indicating a good balance between predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. The standard scaled Wigner matrix and its corresponding semi-circular distribution, particularly its 2kth moment which relates to non-crossing pair-partitions of the set {1, 2,... 2k}, has been extensively studied. Building upon existing knowledge, this paper contributes a broader extension that also reveals novel insights. Given an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix with independently distributed entries under certain assumptions, our study confirms that a limiting spectral distribution indeed exists with probability or certainty. However, this limit can be understood through more extensive partitions, giving rise to intriguing combinatorial problems. As a result, several existing spectral distribution theories, such as those concerning standard Wigner, Erdos-Renyi graph, heavy-tailed Wigner, and variance-profile Wigner matrices, can be derived or further refined. Furthermore, this paper provides conditions under which the spectral distribution approach can lead to new limits or existing limits with a different degree of precision. For instance, we establish the feasibility of spectral distribution around the origin or at the edge for variance-profile Wigner matrices. Additionally, this paper introduces an new method to determine the precision of spectral distribution, enabling us to conclude the empirical spectral distribution of a matrix with independently distributed entries indeed converges to a limit with a specific probability. This probability can be any value within the interval (0,1), and we are confident that this conclusion holds true almost certainly. Almost sure convergence can be demonstrated for real symmetric matrices with independently distributed entries under certain conditions. Consequently, this paper's broader framework for limit spectral distribution can be applied to heavy-tailed Wigner, Erdos-Renyi graph, standard Wigner, and variance-profile Wigner matrices. Moreover, our study on limit spectral distribution can be extended to complex matrices, and we are exploring possible connections to free probability theory. Ultimately, this paper's broader framework can be seen as a more comprehensive theory of limit spectral distribution for a broad class of standard Wigner matrices and their related combinatorial structures. This paper's results on limit spectral distribution also raise further questions and potential applications across various fields. Finally, this paper contributes an new spectral distribution approach based on combinatorial problems, and we are confident that this approach can be used to investigate other complex systems and matrices. This paper's findings on limit spectral distribution demonstrate the power of combinatorial problems in mathematics and our team's expertise in this area. Consequently, we are better equipped to tackle other challenging problems in mathematics and complex systems and we are exploring potential solutions to at least one other problem.

The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. The framework is highly adaptable and responsive to researcher input, enabling us to incorporate new methods for evaluating learning episodes and efficiently manage the challenging balance between exploring and exploiting established approaches. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons. We propose the use of our approach in improving the precision of optical communication system demonstrations that utilize bi-photon sources. Our results also reveal a novel application for the two-dimensionally entangled bi-photon state, enabling the SPADE of previously unaccessible features. Finally, our work facilitates the exploration of quantum aspects of optical communication systems through classical measurements, providing a new means by which to showcase the unique properties of such systems. Experimental implementation of our concept has been successfully achieved. Our study further highlights the value of combining quantum information science and optical communication system technologies. Lastly, our findings have been verified through numerical simulations and an experimental setup is available in the associated repository. The aforementioned implementation has yielded measurable evidence in support of our theoretical findings. Moreover, our study has paved the way for exploring other complex optical field configurations using our novel SPADE approach. In addition to its technological implications, our work has enabled the exploration of unique quantum states through classical optical measurements. While our study has focused on optical communications, our approach may also be applicable to other fields where SPADE can enhance the performance of sub-wavelength scaled devices. In conclusion, our research has successfully overcome a crucial limitation imposed by the Rayleigh criterion in optical systems that measure intensity in the far field. Furthermore, our results have demonstrated the utility of two-dimensionally entangled bi-photon states in optical communications over multiple dimensions. Our study has also facilitated the exploration of quantum aspects of optical communication systems through classical measurements. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. These results highlight the significance of considering the specific mechanisms underlying population interactions and the unique features they introduce. Moreover, this study provides a theoretical framework for identifying early warning signs of population changes and shifts in ecosystem dynamics. Finally, this work emphasizes the value of numerical solutions in confirming theoretical predictions and the importance of distinct time scales in capturing the complex behavior exhibited by species interactions. It also highlights the statistical challenges associated with recognizing the model's early warning signs and the necessity to consider the model's intrinsic variability when attempting to detect these indicators. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. This behavior is likely linked to the formation of massive, compact bulges that hinder further star formation. These findings suggest that the downturn of the mass-star formation rate relation is closely tied to the role of bulges in galaxy evolution. A connection also exists with the transition from a disk-dominated to a bulge-dominated formation history in galaxies, marking a milestone in the assembly of massive galaxies. A similar relation between bulge growth and the downturn of the mass-star formation rate relation has been observed at higher redshifts, which could provide valuable insights into the early formation and evolution of massive galaxies. However, a more detailed analysis of galaxies at $z=1$ is necessary to fully understand the processes involved. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, allowing it to handle multiple fence types with distinct costs. The ability to optimize total fence cost rather than mere count complicates the optimization process. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a prototype implementation has been executed across a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. The performance of resulting programs, equipped with optimally placed fences, has also been simulated. The obtained outcomes show that the counter to the long-standing open question of whether there exists a polynomial-time solvable case for optimal fence set selection with multiple types has been positively answered. The optimized program performance comes close to the ideal, fence-free program performance. The improvement margin varies greatly across different programs, encompassing both simple and complex cases. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zwang84/SABRA. Our model achieves 24.83% mAP on VQA-Det Val, 26.67% mAP on Visual Genome Val, and 26.39% mAP on Visual Genome Test, surpassing the previous best results by 1.03%, 0.17%, and 0.57% mAP respectively. Our analysis indicates that detecting relationships like "play a sport" at (x1,x2) = (person,sport) is 5 times harder than (x1,x2) = (person,football) due to spatial ambiguity, confirming our balanced sampling approach and method enhancements. We have developed a comprehensive model that enables simulation of the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process. It can predict real-world observations and outcomes in scenarios involving linear channel loss, including the associated gain levels, error rates in different measurement bases, and final key rates. Our model is versatile and can be applied to various MDI-QKD implementations that employ convex source states or diverse coding techniques. As such, it is an invaluable resource for analyzing and evaluating the performance of different MDI-QKD protocols. Furthermore, our model facilitates the investigation of novel source states or coding strategies by theoretically simulating the associated technical requirements of real-world MDI-QKD implementations. Building upon our model, we examine and optimize several proposed entanglement purification protocols (EPPs) that target the enhancement of key rate in MDI-QKD systems. Our analysis reveals that the performance of these EPPs heavily relies on the degree of source state multiplexing (SSM). While some EPPs can achieve a significant gain in key rate when SSM is possible, they may struggle to improve key rate in scenarios with low gain levels due to channel loss, ultimately resulting in inferior outcomes. Our model also demonstrates the ineffectiveness of several proposed EPPs for the enhancement of key rate in MDI-QKD systems. Additionally, we examine the impact of distinct coding approaches on the performance of quantum communication systems. Notably, we find that the variable-code quantum key distribution (VC-QKD) protocol, which incorporates diverse coding strategies, can achieve a higher key rate than the conventional single-code MDI-QKD system. However, the actual improvement in key rate varies significantly depending on the specific variable codes employed and the resulting trade-offs between the associated gain levels and error rates. As such, there is considerable headroom for further optimization of variable codes to yield greater gains in key rate. Building upon our model, we investigate several proposed applications of VC-QKD, including the enhancement of key rate in MDI-QKD systems through the use of variable codes that can tolerate distinct levels of channel loss. Our findings indicate that VC-QKD can yield better practical outcomes than the conventional single-code MDI-QKD system, resulting in a greater improvement in key rate in scenarios with low gain levels due to linear channel loss. Notably, we demonstrate that the proposed paradoxical variable codes, which can achieve a higher key rate than the conventional single-code MDI-QKD system, can perform remarkably well in scenarios with low gain levels due to linear channel loss.

Advancements in machine learning and signal processing have generated substantial interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which excel at solving complex, engineering-driven problems. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. This study aims to offer a thorough exploration into comprehending, visualizing, and explicating the inner workings and global behavior of DNNs. We gather and examine previous research on topic-specific subsets of neural networks, cover various visualization methods that reveal the structural and temporal dynamics of models, discuss ways to measure the reliability of DNN outputs, present methods for quantifying a network's performance and contribution in multi-layer architectures, and finally, discuss diverse techniques for understanding the global behavior of DNNs, including their general performance, sensitivity to hyperparameters, and the effect of specific data points on the learning process. We hope this exhaustive survey will serve as a foundational resource for investigating the complex, underlying phenomena of DNN learning and behavior and will motivate future research in the XAI field. In addition, we include a summary of our key findings, a thorough examination of the methods' scope and their statistical performance, as well as a discussion on how to further advance the field of XAI through the effective use of techniques like gradient-free optimization and representation learning. Ultimately, we outline a research roadmap for exploring the comprehension, visualization, and explanation of DNNs across multiple domains and advocate for the incorporation of high-level system perspectives in future modeling applications. This will enable the development of more robust and adaptable models that are better equipped to handle complex, dynamic scenarios. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, the system's capacity to minimize the required data and avoid overfitting in real-world applications is also verified. The implementation of the system's code is available at https://github.com/sierra24/MetaFEND. This system has the potential to enhance the accuracy of fake news detection in practical applications and serves as a platform for further development in the field. This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison between discrete and continuous AoI is provided, including mean values for the M/M/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that the standard queueing theory is capable of analyzing the discrete AoI, outperforming previously proposed methods for continuous time systems. Finally, we investigate the optimal control of AoI in the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We show that a control strategy based on the last transition time can achieve the optimal performance, and we derive the optimal policy for the M/M/1/1 queue. This is further extended to obtain the optimal threshold for the geometrically distributed service time. We conclude by discussing recent contributions and future research directions for the discrete-time status updating system. Additionally, we explore the relevance of these results to systems following the G/Ge/1/1 queue. We provide the final answer for the mean AoI of the M/M/1/1 queue and identify areas for further improvement of the established performance bounds. Lastly, we examine the implications of our findings on the analysis of the G/Ge/1/1 queue. Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Omnidirectional precoding applications in five-dimensional GCM pairs are also explored. A simple permutation-based phase rotation technique is proposed and is effective in pairs of non-full-rank GCMs. A more comprehensive analysis on this technique is planned for future work. A simple approach to create a GCM from a GCM quad is also presented and a few more instances of GCM quadruples are generated using this method. A key observation from this study is that all the constructed GCM quadruples share a key property: their elements are all binary. A method for constructing binary GCM quadruples is proposed and it is hypothesized that all positive integers can be represented as sums of four binary numbers with specific properties, which is confirmed for integers up to 1000. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon. Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. In particular, we applied this concept to analyze the performance of a grid-based electric distribution network, showcasing the potential of this approach to enhance monitoring and control systems by detecting unusual behavior in a new area. The techniques developed in this research can be seen as a significant breakthrough in combining modern machine learning methods with complex system analysis, offering a new framework that can be readily explored in innumerable domains and scenarios. Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research, and their strong quantum nonlocality is therefore a topic of interest. However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. In this research, a series of UPBs of various larger sizes for systems of three and four parties were constructed in dimensions of $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D \geq 3$. It was also shown that these UPBs have strong quantum nonlocality, answering open questions from Halder and others, and providing a connection between this phenomenon and UPBs. To locally distinguish one such UPB in $3 \otimes 3 \otimes 4$, an entanglement-assisted protocol was proposed, using less entanglement than previously known protocols. Additionally, a lower bound for the number of states in a UPB that demonstrates strong quantum nonlocality was derived, and some UPBs were found to have a near-optimal number of such states. Finally, a method was described for converting certain UPBs into ones that demonstrate strong quantum nonlocality, and several natural challenges were identified in this area of research. System of three parties can be thought of as a child of systems of two parties, and therefore much of this research can be seen as answering open questions from Halder and others. In addition to its fundamental importance, this phenomenon may also have practical uses in the development of unextendible bases and other protocols. Furthermore, this research provides a new perspective on the relationship between UPBs and other multipartite states, and it is expected to have implications for future studies in this area. The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the initial conditions are met, the algorithm achieves full convergence. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue. Finally, the algorithm's performance is validated in a real-world testing environment. The completed astrobots are then put into operation at the SDSS-V's KOi-1111b field and collect data at a rate comparable to the standard SDSS-IV workflow. The study's findings are applicable to other safe coordination applications. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. Additionally, a new version of the compiler called GP 4B is introduced, derived from the GP 4 compiler that supports multiple types of graphs and user-defined values. GP 4B serves as the most advanced version of the GP 2 compiler, incorporating a range of innovations while demonstrating exceptional efficiency in compiling programs for various applications, including program analysis and verification. Two use cases are presented to illustrate GP 4B's capabilities, highlighting its potential as a leading compiler for graph-based programs. However, a few notable challenges remain in GP 4B development, primarily related to the compilation of referentially functional programs and the incorporation of static type checking, both of which pose significant obstacles. To address these issues, novel solutions such as the introduction of reference fields in the graph data structure and the integration of type checking into the compiler front-end have been explored, along with the benefits and limitations of these approaches. Furthermore, the opportunity exists for the exploration of other compiler architectures in relation to GP 4B, primarily due to the compiler's straightforward design. This, along with the availability of the GP 4B source code and the GP 2 framework, provides a foundation for the development of advanced program analysis and verification tools. Finally, the challenge is raised for future research to focus on the integration of program proof and verification into the GP 4B compiler, offering potential avenues for exploration. This master's thesis work contributes significantly to the GP 2 compiler research, addressing key challenges and paving the way for the development of efficient and innovative program analysis and verification tools. Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. Furthermore, our framework's potential in feature selection is also illustrated. Our research provides a groundbreaking approach that advances the understanding of contrastive learning in feature extraction. The integrated of unsupervised and supervised learning techniques within a single framework is a key innovation. The framework's potential to enhance feature extraction performance paves the way for its potential application in other machine learning contexts. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. Notably, our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques for model selection and sparse modeling on the UCI dataset by a significant margin. Additionally, our method is applicable to various loss functions, including the squared error and absolute error. Finally, our method is implemented in the R package glasso2step, available on CRAN. Unlike other methods, our method does not rely on an initial consistent estimate of the group Lasso, allowing it to handle large datasets and reducing memory usage by approximately 50%. Furthermore, our method enables easy clustering of models using anelbow, allowing it to determine the optimal model size quickly. Finally, our method can also be used for feature selection using the BIC information criterion. Additionally, our method is currently being extended to handle neural networks. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed. Furthermore, novel approaches for estimating distortion and focal length were successfully evaluated, reducing the estimated mean and maximum errors by 45% and 25% respectively in certain scenarios. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models. In particular, this work highlights the potential of marmoset-based midscale brain modeling, demonstrating that such models can accurately replicate aspects of larger primate brains. As research progresses, the model will be refined and used to investigate multiple aspects of the marmoset Parkinson's disease brain, including distinct stages of dopaminergic neuron loss and the effects of different treatment interventions. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Furthermore, we show that quantum entanglement can be confirmed and even characterized through analysis of optical tomogram correlations, while synchronization can be proven by examining the cross-correlation of two synchronized states. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. To facilitate
further research, we have made our data sets and models available publicly. We
believe that incorporating role specifications can enhance the performance of open-
domain dialogue systems and may also be applicable to other natural language
processing tasks with specifications on text composition. Additionally, our work
has implications for the broad range of NLP applications involving human-machine
interactions, such as customer support systems, virtual assistants, and chatbots.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data. Moreover, the conventional method solely considers farmer profitability, disregarding the influence of disease pressure on yields and profit. To address these challenges, we developed a method using simulations to account for a limited number of observations and incorporated disease pressure's effect through a quantile regression model, applying this solution to strawberry disease management in Florida. The results showed that, despite the limited sample size, the method effectively compared treatment efficiency across different disease pressure levels, revealing that the least efficient treatment at the 10th quantile became significantly less efficient at the 90th quantile due to its greater vulnerability to subpar yields under extreme disease pressure conditions. This method can serve as a framework for research on the economic evaluation of pest management strategies. Additionally, we explored correlations between the results obtained through stochastic analysis and field data, finding that the most efficient treatment identified through our method consistently performed better than the least efficient one in actual experiments, albeit the difference in efficiency was statistically significant only for one of the three variables considered. Moreover, we observed that the least efficient treatment performed significantly worse under optimal disease pressure conditions and significantly better under severe conditions. This research can provide a foundation for the development of decision-support tools to aid farmers in making informed decisions about pesticide use, crop management, and biological control program participation. It is also essential for academics to engage with agricultural industry representatives and provide practical solutions to real-world problems. As a result, we derive inequalities including an anisotropic Willmore inequality, a sharp anisotropic Minkowski inequality, and a sharp volumetric anisotropic Minkowski inequality. Our proof involves a novel approach in nonlinear potential theory recently described in the reference provided. This approach enables us to formulate a key inequality as a consequence of a compact embedding theorem for specific Sobolev spaces. In the context of the anisotropic Minkowski inequality, this approach yields a direct proof of the inequality's sharpness. Additionally, we demonstrate that the anisotropic Minkowski inequality can be modified to account for volumetric constraints. This modification results in a broader inequality covering cases where the target shape has a non-zero anisotropic Minkowski volume equal to that of the original shape. This research addresses open questions posed by Scheeffer and by Kenig and Nangia. Firstly, we confirm that the sharp anisotropic Minkowski inequality holds for convex areas.

Thirdly, we establish that the sharp anisotropic Minkowski inequality is equivalent to a specific inequality concerning the anisotropic capacity, which solves Problem 2 posed by Kenig and Nangia.
Lastly, we demonstrate that the sharp volumetric anisotropic Minkowski inequality implies a specific inequality concerning the anisotropic capacity, which solves Problem 3 posed by Kenig and Nangia. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Additionally, a general approach is discussed for implicitly defining safe reduction rules, which can be applied to the analysis of parameterized complexity of NP-complete problems. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. For practical applications, we suggest TRAIL, an algorithm that utilizes contrastive learning for energy-based models to derive the action space. The benefits of this approach were verified in experiments on navigation and locomotion tasks, yielding up to a 4x performance improvement compared to baseline imitation learning methods. The code is available at https://github.com/vt-vl-lab/trail. The theoretical analysis proves that our method's success relies on a well-chosen loss function and relevant data sets. This study's findings imply that imitation learning from suboptimal paths can lead to nearly optimal performance. This has implications for topics like airless transfer and few-shot adaptation. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Notably, our approach achieves notable performance gains in cooperative settings. The code for our research is publicly available on the GitHub platform. With inter-agent imitation allowing us to achieve notable progress in reinforcement learning without relying on external expert demonstrations, the potential for future exploration in collaborative learning domains is substantial. In particular, we believe our approach could be a powerful foundation for addressing pivotal challenges in collaborative reinforcement learning, including key issues in multi-agent reward learning and stable concurrent training. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy. Furthermore, our method is capable of adapting to a wider range of poses than previously thought possible with marker-based systems. Additionally, we have found that our method is robust in environments with low lighting and can accurately estimate poses in environments with objects of varying sizes and colors; we have also successfully tested our system on multiple robot setups. Overall, our system offers high precision, robustness, and flexibility, making it well-suited for a variety of applications, including those requiring end-effector trajectory planning and those that rely on object rotation and keypoint location. Full source code for our method can be found at https://github.com/bradleyguo/extrinsic_calibration. Overall, our method excels in precision, robustness, and flexibility, making it suitable for various applications, including end-effector trajectory planning and object rotation and keypoint location-dependent tasks.
