This study introduces two key concepts, quasi-finitely separating maps and quasiapproximate identities, which form the basis for the definitions of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces. Additionally, connections between QFS-spaces and other space types, such as FS-spaces, quasicontinuous spaces, and discrete spaces, are explored, revealing that discrete spaces are subtypes of QFS-spaces and FS-spaces are instances of QFS-spaces in certain scenarios. Furthermore, the concept of closed QFS-spaces is introduced, along with examples illustrating the distinction between closed and non-closed QFS-spaces. Moreover, lattice structure is established for spaces of continuous QFS-spaces and FS-spaces, whereas the lattice structure for spaces of closed QFS-spaces and FS-spaces is demonstrated under specific conditions. Lastly, the notion of upper space structures is used to prove that the collection of QFS-spaces forms a closure operator and forms a lattice once restricted to closed QFS-spaces. This research expands our understanding of continuous and separate map properties and their corresponding space types, while also highlighting the significance of quasicontinuous approximation identities and quasicontinuous map properties. Furthermore, this study offers implications for upper space structures and notable map types, such as the collection of continuous, separate, and closed map bases, the collection of discrete map bases, and the collection of closed map bases. Additionally, this research provides insights into the relationship between continuous, discrete, and closed map bases and whether the collection of continuous map bases forms a monomorphism. Lastly, this study provides a starting point for further exploration into the collection of closed, discrete, and continuous map bases and the structure of the lattice of monomorphisms. We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size. We establish this time complexity to be optimal by demonstrating that the combined cyclic variant of three deterministic context-free languages has a time complexity of at least $n^2$ for solving its complement. Our results provide an alternative explanation for a previous conjecture regarding the time complexity of V's word problem. Our method involves using a binary tree structure, which we term the 'Schweitzer tree', to efficiently solve the combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages. This solution employs a context where a state and a symbol can be replaced by another state and another symbol, subject to specific rules applying to the 'Schweitzer tree'. We establish that any combined cyclic variant of context-free languages can be transformed into an equivalent cycle that only recognizes even lengths, allowing us to restrict our attention to combined cyclic variants of only the deterministic context-free languages. We further prove that solving the combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages is equivalent to solving a related problem involving a stack-based structure, which we term the 'Schweitzer stack'. We show that solving the word problem for V can be achieved by stacking the Schweitzer trees generated by each generator, subject to specific rules. We demonstrate that this method is a direct expression of the group operation in V. We term the method in which the last generator applied is the topmost stack, and the time complexity of this method is the square of the number of stacks. We assume a binary representation for the states and symbols, which allows us to represent each state or symbol as a binary sequence of a fixed length. We assume that the length of each sequence is large enough that the number of possible sequences is a power that is greater than two to a power. because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment. 
This allows for the maintenance of a non-equilibrium steady state that is 
characterized by two-way flow of information, even when the system is in contact 
with a thermal bath and there is rapid loss due to spontaneous emission. 
However, this state requires certain conditions to be met, such as the need for 
the system's interaction with the environment to occur over a time period that 
is much longer than the time it takes for spontaneous emission to occur. 
Our theory includes a time-dependent master equation that can be used to describe 
the situation with rapid loss due to spontaneous emission, and it demonstrates 
that even in this situation, there can still be two-way flow of information, 
provided that the system's state remains entangled with the photon field. 
This technique could potentially be applied to other open systems. 
However, if the system's connection to the environment is based on continuous wave 
fields rather than photons, then there can never be two-way flow of information, 
even if the system's interaction with the environment occurs over a time period that 
is much longer than the time it takes for spontaneous emission to occur. 
This is because continuous wave fields cause a type of decay that is equivalent to 
a constant force rather than a force that varies with time. 
On the other hand, the use of discrete wave fields allows for the creation of a 
time-dependent force that can result in a situation where there can be two-way 
flow of information.

light rather than a constant light.

While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems. Our results also establish the connection between recognisable sets in base p/q and base p/qq systems, revealing that a set is recognisable in base p/q if and only if its corresponding set is recognisable in base ppq/qq. Our research offers insights into both theoretical base system dynamics and potential applications in coding theory. Finally, our work introduces an open question regarding the relationship between sequential and simultaneous recognisable sets in base p/q systems. Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry. The model's parameters are then evaluated through a comprehensive statistical analysis while incorporating multiple constraints including those from neutrino data, the Lyman-alpha forest, geophysical measurements of the axion coupling to baryons, and the cosmic microwave background. The investigation reveals an extremely narrow range for the ratio of the sterile-neutrino to the axion's thermal ab initio multiplicity, and thus a single parameter governs the abundance of both the axion and the sterile neutrino. The model also predicts an extremely low effective mass for the sterile neutrino of $keV\sim 10^{3}$, and thus it fails to account for the recent ozone anomaly observed at the LHC, and also falls short of meeting the experimental requirements needed to validate it through the GeHZI experiment at the LHC. The model however does provide a basis for its extension in a multplicity of ways. Finally, we conclude by highlighting the model's ability to be tested through the detection of sterile neutrinos and axion particles such as two photon decays, and we also outline a strategy for testing its validity through both the LHC and a new particle physics initiative referred to as the "Future Circular Collider". This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances and extinction values. Ultimately, the LAMOST research team constructed a binary catalog of around 2,700 candidates through the analysis of their light curves, radial velocity fitting, the extraction of binarity parameters from medium-resolution spectra, and cross-referencing it with the $Gaia$ EDR3 binary catalog. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. The enhanced results demonstrate the potential of the EG-CNN to serve as a versatile, universally applicable module in various image analysis tasks. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. To achieve this, we developed a method that involves translating the pseudocode representations of these protocols into statements describing their behavior, and subsequently using a static analysis technique to prove the consistency guarantees implied by these statements. Ultimately, our work confirms that MongoDB's transaction protocols provide the consistency guarantees stated in the official documentation, and our approach can be applied to the analysis of other database transaction protocols. Our verification results have been made available as an independent repository that can serve as a reference for the transaction protocols used in MongoDB and its related deployments. Furthermore, this repository includes examples of how to use the protocol specifications for purposes other than verification. In addition, we discuss the implications of our findings on the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's document-store architecture, and propose an alternative design that could provide strict consistency in certain use cases. Our approach has been successfully applied to the verification of MongoDB's transaction protocols, and the benefits of this approach have been demonstrated through the development of a prototype of a distributed database that is based on the specifications of MongoDB's transaction protocols and provides efficient performance in benchmark tests. In particular, our results show that the prototype database performs within a factor of two of the best-performing databases in the YCSB benchmark, and achieves linear scalability in certain workloads. Overall, our work has shown that the transaction protocols used in MongoDB and its related deployments are consistent with the guarantees stated in the official documentation, and has demonstrated the effectiveness of a method that combines formal specification and verification in the development of reliable and efficient database transaction protocols. Additionally, our work has been recognized by the database community, and has inspired further research into the development of reliable and efficient database systems. The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Our research lays the foundation for further exploration into developing methods to mitigate the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/yousefis/BiasDetectionFramework.  Our study has been conducted in accordance with the standards of the Clinical Artificial Intelligence Norms coalition and the guidelines set by the Institutional Review Board. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder. The findings suggest that static and dynamic properties of nanoscale assemblies can be finely tuned to mimic critical phenomena observed in larger systems, providing a new means to control self-organized behavior through spatial interaction topology. The methods employed in this research could also be applied to other models featuring triangle-based interactions to reveal the hidden geometric effects on dynamical processes occurring within complex networks. The associated code can be found at: https://github.com/alexsantoro/selforganizedcriticality-attriples. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical than expected and followed a linear relationship with the temperature and density of the surrounding plasma, which is not evident in the data from further out in the solar system. Additionally, we found the critical energy flux for preventing coronal mass ejections from occurring was about twice the average required to balance the gravitational force of mass ejection, and this average varied significantly over the data collection period, but always remained higher than the flux that could reach the solar surface and balance gravity with energy alone. Lastly, we established that the linear relationship between energy flux and the temperature and density of the surrounding plasma held true, but only if we used the density and temperature at the edge of the solar magnetic field's sheath, rather than the values measured further out in the plasma stream. This finding points to the importance of plasma behavior in the very intimate space near the solar surface, but more precise observations are needed to fully understand the underlying processes. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our study employs nuclear forward scattering with the $^{151}$Eu nuclear moment,  allowing us to probe pressure-induced changes in the electronic state and crystal structure and ultimately understand the pressure behavior of this material.  Initially, BFTO exhibits ferromagnetic characteristics at low temperatures and a N\'{e}el temperature of 650 molebars (6.5 MPa) bar before transitioning to an antiferromagnetic configuration above this threshold under high-pressure conditions. We observe the reorientation of spin in BFTO to be influenced by both the lattice structural changes and the competition between direct and super-superexchange interactions, ultimately affecting its magnetic properties. Hybrid methods tackling continuous shortest path problems start by local optimization
of discrete shortest paths in spatial networks. The convergence to optimal solutions
depends on the discretization error caused by restricting the global search to a network,
with specific implications on the choice of network density. A notable application
is flight planning, which involves determining optimal routes considering factors such
as flight time, fuel consumption, and weather conditions. Advanced algorithms for
discrete shortest paths can be used to compute starting points for locally convergent
methods in optimal control. We establish a priori and localized bounds for the
error in estimated flight times compared to optimal continuous trajectories, taking
into account network density and wind field. These bounds facilitate designing
networks with optimal connectivity, and the derived bounds are illustrated through
benchmarks, which show significant improvements in localization but still offer scope
for refinement through additional estimators. The proposed methods are relevant to
a broad range of applications involving discrete-continuous shortest paths. For flight
planning, the bounds are specifically evaluated up to 500 km in a 1000 km^2 area with
wind speeds of 50 km/h. The implemented algorithms are made available as part of the
Trajectory Optimization Library (TOL).  We introduce an open issue on integrating
machine learning algorithms for network planning, encouraging researchers to contribute
their work.  Finally, we present an application involving the optimization of a virtual
satellite mission.  We outline future research directions, including (but not limited to)
the development of more sophisticated preconditioning techniques, the investigation of alternative
discrete shortest path algorithms, and a deeper examination of wind models.  Additionally, we provide an updated version of the paper addressing a reviewer's comment.  This updated version includes an corrected statement regarding the comparison of our bounds to existing work, and clarifies the methodology used for the evaluation of flight planning algorithms.  Furthermore, we include an expanded discussion on the limitations of our approach and future research directions in the field of optimal control.  The revised paper includes an updated reference to a recent publication, and the accompanying code has been updated to reflect these changes.  The code for the paper's experiments can be found at  https://github.com/lschneider18/tol/tree/v1.1.1, and the paper itself can be downloaded from  https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.15031. In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental analysis reveals the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, can be manipulated by adjusting a gate. The observed switching probability distributions are in line with minimal capacitance and moderate resistance, causing the switching current to be only a small portion of the critical current. Furthermore, synchronization between two JJs can cause a disparity in the switching current when comparing measurements of a single JJ versus that same JJ within an asymmetrical SQUID loop, where T* can be fine-tuned through applied magnetic flux. The flux-dependent T* follows a 2π-fold periodic pattern, and the chance of observing a specific parity of the phase dynamics depends on the average phase angle at the time of switching. The unique properties of planar JJs make them suitable for implementing fault-tolerant quantum computations employing the adiabatic processing model. The work presented here contributes to a comprehensive understanding of phase dynamics in planar JJs and SQUIDs. The experimental analysis of our findings, facilitated by switching current probability distributions, offers a direct and accessible method for evaluating the capacitance, resistance, and critical current of a single JJ, or these quantities in one of the loop's component SQUIDs. The research provides a foundation for exploring the execution of quantum operations and the resulting state evolution in epitaxial planar superconducting processors. The study demonstrates the capability to implement multi-gate quantum electronics, wherein the outcome of quantum operations depends on the intersection of multiple applied magnetic fields and electric potentials. The work presented a prototype for a multi-gate quantum computer that serves as a time-domain controller, overseeing the execution of quantum operations through a single combined gate, achieving a combined effect comparable to that achieved with multiple individual gates. The study also introduces the novel concept of multi-gate quantum electronics, demonstrating its potential to enhance the efficiency of quantum communications protocols, such as coherent state communications, involving the encoding of multiple bits within a single optical state. The work presented a protocol for detecting the combined effect of multiple gates and demonstrated a combined multiplier of proportional to the square of the number of gates. The study also introduced a new threshold, that of the quantum electronics threshold, that characterizes the combined effect of multiple gates and offered a new means of controlling quantum operations through a single combined gate, dependent on the quantum electronics threshold and the specific implementation of the quantum processor.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, demonstrating that the limit functional comprises two components: the stored energy within the matrix, and the stored energy within the fillings. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. Interestingly, our results indicate that the proposed algorithm can achieve a similar level of solution accuracy when compared to other optimization methods, despite the presence of malicious agents. This has important implications for the design of robust and efficient optimization algorithms in complex multi-agent systems. 

In a collaborative optimization setting involving multiple agents, the behavior of some agents may negatively impact the achievement of optimal solutions due to their deceptive information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we present a novel approach based on gradient updates, along with a quantized communication method. This approach is mathematically proven to result in solutions that converge to the optimal solution at a rate defined by $O(1/\sqrt{k})$. The effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy are quantified, along with a broader application of this approach to convex optimization problems. Our studies demonstrate that the proposed algorithm performs comparably to other optimization methods, despite the presence of malicious agents. This has important implications for the design of robust and efficient optimization algorithms in complex multi-agent systems.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package's capabilities are demonstrated using data from the QUBIC experiment; however, it can be adapted to other similar experiments with only minor adjustments required. The code is openly available on GitHub, allowing users to explore its functionality and make their own modifications as needed. Furthermore, the paper discusses the practical applications of using simulated data to evaluate the performance of flight instruments, such as QUBIC and CMB-S4, as well as future ground-based and balloon-borne experiments. The approach presented in this paper can also be expanded to incorporate other systematics and cross-correlation analyses. The code's user manual is included in the supplementary materials provided with this paper. The package is available for use in the QUBIC and CMB-S4 communities; however, its general functionality makes it applicable to any similar cosmic microwave background experiment based on bolometric technology. The code has been openly contributed to the instrument science suite developed for CMB-S4, as a result of which it will be an official part of that platform. The package has also been incorporated into the QUBIC data analysis pipeline, and will be used to validate the performance of its front-end system during data reduction and archiving. The code has been successfully tested on local high-performance computing resources and is now being integrated into the UK Arts and Humanities Research Council's (AHRC) share of the NSF-funded, University of Colorado Denver-led allocation of time on the IBM ACI I cluster, which is part of the US Department of Energy's (DOE) supercomputer system at the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC). In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. We also introduce an intuitive explanation for this phenomenon based on the relative distribution of remaining degrees in the LDPC degree distribution, providing a simple framework for designing optimized degree schedules. This approach may be adapted to other density-dependent transmission channels. We anticipate our explorations to contribute significantly to the ongoing quest to create LDPC codes resistant to various types of errors. In addition, our study may offer insights beneficial to the broader research community working on unequal error protection strategies. We anticipate our findings to be of particular interest to scientists studying the performance of computer network systems prone to errors. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states. Our analysis also reveals that the security hazard persists even if the phase randomness is increased to a certain point. Our proposed attack can be implemented using a minimal set of technical complexities compared to other hacking strategies. To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in edge computing and communication energy consumption, promoting energy self-sustainability in MNs through the use of green energy sources. The integration of thinking in the network architecture is also likely to result in increased robustness to failures and extended lifespan of edge computing devices. The proposals made in this paper can contribute to the development of self-organized and sustainable 5G and Future MNs. This involves designing and implementing an energy-efficient edge computing system at a 5G BN in the University of Surrey Campus. In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, we explore the notion that the definition of angle function equivalent to the one proposed by Menger can be derived from the definition based on betweenness, which implies that the previously known solutions to his problems are a corollary of this relationship. Additionally, we establish that the concept of angle function, when defined using betweenness, finds applications in order structures and serves as a primary reason for classifying certain spaces with the property of betweenness as semi-metric and metric spaces. Building on this, we also prove that angle-preserving functions between spaces with the property of betweenness preserve betweenness, which in turn allows us to demonstrate the homeomorphism between specific types of closed subspaces of Euclidean planes. Lastly, we conclude that the recent solution to the first of Menger's problems, which states that any closed subspace of a Euclidean plane can be embedded with the angle function onto a closed subspace of another Euclidean plane, has far-reaching implications. This includes the fact that the category of closed subspaces of Euclidean planes is not equivalent to the category of closed subspaces of hyperbolic planes. This article further explores the category of closed subspaces of Euclidean and hyperbolic planes with the angle function, which provides a new perspective on the problem of embedding spaces with the angle function into the structure of Euclidean and hyperbolic planes. Building upon this, we establish that any topological group can be embedded with the angle function onto a subspace of a Euclidean plane. This, in turn, allows us to demonstrate that any topological group can be embedded with the angle function onto a subspace of a hyperbolic plane. Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. The robustness of DR-DSGD is demonstrated through an extensive evaluation of $15$ applications across $5$ datasets in independent experiments. We have examined past methods of computing pressure for the hard-disk model, dating back to 1953, and contrasted these with results we obtained through a powerful simulation technique and a highly efficient algorithm that leverages many computer processors simultaneously. Like various simple scientific models, such as the Drosophila model, understanding the hard-disk model required significant effort. In our research, we argue that the difficulty of measuring the pressure has not been fully acknowledged in the long-standing debate regarding the hard-disk phase-transition scenario. Our paper provides the fundamental principles of the hard-disk model, defines the concept of pressure and presents new, unbiased methods of estimating it. Additionally, we explore different computational algorithms used for sampling and discuss critical factors that affect how quickly they reach equilibrium in the absence of theoretical guidance. Our findings, specifically pressure values calculated for up to one million disks, can serve as a benchmark for evaluating future simulation methods. Moreover, we make publicly accessible, in an open-source database, both pressure data and different variations of the used simulation methods and pressure estimation algorithms. This database is accessible via an open-source tool called HardDiskDB, which we introduced alongside our research. HardDiskDB encompasses not only our pressure results but also a vast array of simulation models that can be appraised using the described pressure estimation methods. This database addresses a significant shortcoming in computer simulations used for studying out-of-equilibrium systems and provides a valuable resource for both scientific and technological applications. This encompasses high-performance benchmarking, a significant computational challenge that can be achieved with our simulation methods. By incorporating pressure, a critical system property, this metric offers a more holistic evaluation of computational systems than previously available methods. This new 'pressure metric' has been incorporated into HardDiskDB along with our research findings. This database provides an invaluable resource not only for understanding the hard-disk model but also for evaluating the performance of computer processors in a more comprehensive way than ever before. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been difficult until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. Additionally, we suggested that two of the open clusters shared a common metal composition with the galaxy's bulge, and that further study was necessary to resolve the composition of the third. We also found that the location, motion, and metal composition of one of the open clusters, VVV-CL063, matched that of the nearby RR Lyrae star field, and that the motion of another, VVV-CL160, was unusual but needed further investigation, and that the third, VVV-CL174, contained a red horizontal branch that was either composed of two separate clusters or had an abnormally low metal content. We recommended that further research, such as analyzing light from these clusters at different wavelengths, be conducted to better understand their composition and structure. This particular research centers around the Drell-Yan process and focuses on vector-boson transverse momentum, $q_T$, and beam thrust, $\mathcal T$, to illustrate exclusive observable behavior. Our analysis addresses the various scale relationships in differential distributions ranging from massless $m \ll q_T$ to heavy-quark dominant decoupling limit $q_T \ll m$. To investigate quark-mass dependencies accurately within intermediate regime $m \sim q_T$, it necessitates a consideration of beam and soft functions as mass dependent entities. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. We anticipate that this finding will contribute to the better understanding and development of efficient TB models capable of capturing the complexities of light-matter interactions. Moreover, our work showcases the potential of Wannier models to integrate matrix elements that facilitate the integration of TB models with optical experiments, thereby providing a comprehensive framework for the simulation of quantum dynamics under electromagnetic fields. This approach can serve as a blueprint for the development of accurate TB models applicable to a broad spectrum of materials and phenomena. Additionally, our research may facilitate the development of efficient and accurate TB models, which will, in turn, enable the simulation of high-field quantum dynamics and strong-field laser-matter interactions. We believe that our work will be relevant to a diverse range of scientific communities, including physics, chemistry, materials science, and physics of nanostructures and quantum technologies. Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for planetary habitability assessments. However, the limited wavelength range of these observations restricts analysis to energy release during the coolest post-flare phase. In contrast, ground-based near-ultraviolet (NUV) observations, which cover a different spectral range, combine with optical data to gain a comprehensive understanding of white-light stellar flares. We present a detailed analysis of the 1985 April 12 superflare from AD Leo using archival NUV and optical light curves, which shows a significant contrast with post-flare phases observed by space missions. Instead, the NUV and optical light curves exhibit a ~3-day recovery period, offering a wider spectral range than previously observed and potentially linked to the presence of electrons generated during the flare's active phase. Our research emphasizes the importance of continued NUV photometric observations from space missions like Kepler, particularly for evaluating a star's suitability for supporting life on planets in its habitable zone. In addition, we recommend astronomers, researchers, and scientists to submit proposals for observing stars that host exoplanets in the NUV band to gain a more in-depth understanding of white-light stellar flares. In conclusion, combined NUV and optical data analysis provides a more comprehensive understanding of white-light stellar flares, highlighting the need for continued observation of these astronomical phenomena in the NUV spectrum. Furthermore, we present a statistical analysis of all published and observed NUV light curves from AD Leo and DW Leo, which show a higher contrast with a shorter post-flare recovery period than the majority of post-flare phases observed by space missions. In addition, we outline a novel method for calculating the flare's full width at half minimum intensity, a crucial parameter for evaluating the energy released during the flare's active phase, and provide results for the 1985 April 12 superflare from AD Leo. Additionally, we present a discussion on the potential link between the observed differences in contrast and recovery periods and the various energy release mechanisms that govern different post-flare phases. In conclusion, combined NUV and optical data analysis provide a more comprehensive understanding of white-light stellar flares, highlighting the need for continued observation of these astronomical phenomena in the NUV spectrum. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. This research introduces a cutting-edge algorithm that enables clustering of dynamic systems at a linear and non-linear level, and showcases its versatility through seamless adaptation to linear and non-linear transmission networks as well as atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. This algorithm boasts a low computational footprint, achievable on a desktop computer. Further, this study explores the correlation between clustering results and the system's parameters, revealing that its effectiveness is finely tuned by the clustering algorithm's parameters, the time-series data duration, and the state similarity threshold. This insight holds significant value in modeling and controlling across domains. This research is a significant contribution in the field of control theory, particularly in systems research, and provides a groundbreaking solution to the longstanding problem of identifying communities within complex systems. Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Ultimately, our study recommends employing the integrated model for population density estimations when data are available.  If only capture data are available, we advise using our method that utilizes capture-recapture models alone for population density estimations, acknowledging that doing so results in slightly inferior precision estimations.  In any case, our results encourage the use of capture data in conjunction with spatial capture-recapture models that incorporate resource selection functions to explore animals' spatial behavior.  We believe our method offers a useful framework for researching the complex relationships between animals and their environment.  To facilitate the implementation of our method, we have incorporated it into a R program that is attached to this article along with an example dataset available on the journal website.  We hope this will facilitate the adoption of our statistical method by other researchers working in this field.  We have explored the method's performance using simulated data but not yet tested it with real telemetry data due to the large file size restrictions imposed by the journal.  We have derived the theoretical basis for model integration but not assessed the method's applicability to animals that occupy spaces with fractal characteristics.  Therefore, we have been unable to utilize revenue generated by the previous publication to support field studies that could provide further insight into the animal's spatial occupancy behavior.

To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations. Our study demonstrates that HiP-RSSMs can adapt to unknown dynamic scenarios and effectively utilize shared state variables to make accurate predictions. By leveraging shared state variables, HiP-RSSMs achieved a significant margin in accuracy over traditional state-space models, especially in scenarios with rapidly changing dynamics. Additionally, HiP-RSSMs proved to be a strong multi-task learner, surpassing models that used shared initial conditions and latent variables. We associated these patterns with the method's success and identified key characteristics that contributed to its decline in performance. Finally, we introduced a new challenge, the multi-task state-space model challenge, and demonstrated that HiP-RSSMs can solve complex, real-world problems in robotics by solving a smaller-scale version of this challenge. Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ is then described as acting on the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$. It has previously been shown that two vectors in the representation space of $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$, which are expressible as linear combinations of elements of the form $e_\alpha$, are equivalent to one another. This proof is now extended to the situation where the root system $\Phi$ is of type $B_l$. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Our code, dubbed CTTK, is an open-source contribution to the Einstein Toolkit. We present numerical results that validate our method's effectiveness. Furthermore, we observe that using a simple 'blueberry' conformal field configuration, which mimics the behavior of particles under the influence of gravity, does not significantly impact the solutions obtained through this method. This technique emerges as a more pragmatic approach for resolving the initial data constraints in numerical simulations of numerical relativity. Additionally, we explore the implications of our method for simulations involving scalar fields and the role of conformal field configurations, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive understanding of how these configurations relate to physical phenomena in general relativity. This work is a result of the efforts of the Numerical Relativity Science Group at the University of Tennessee. Our code is built upon the Einstein Toolkit and features an innovative strategy that solves the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints as a combined system. This combined approach results in a solution of one constraint depending on the other, thus avoiding the typical application of an iterative multigrid solver. Our code consists of two main components: a combined solver for the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints and a suite of tests that demonstrate our method's performance and accuracy. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our results demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is directly proportional to the conductivity coefficient and an external magnetic field has a minimal influence on the anomalous Nernst effect in this material. Notably, we discovered that an increased spin-polarization-driven transverse thermal transport can exceed the normal thermal transport component, resulting in a significant thermomagnetic force and potentially enriching the functional capabilities of these materials in thermomagnetic devices. Our research further reveals that the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN can be adjusted through changes in the surface plasmon resonance of a adjacent metal layer, offering a practical method for the design and optimization of these materials for various applications. Our study provides valuable insights that can guide the further exploration of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials and proposes a method for controlling this phenomenon. Additionally, our research demonstrates the utility of measuring the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects simultaneously, an approach that can be applied to a broad range of materials exhibiting the anomalous Hall effect. Furthermore, we introduce a new non-invasive approach for determining the anomalous Nernst coefficient and demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately measuring this quantity in Mn$_3$NiN. Our research also explores the energy-related applications of these materials and suggests opportunities for further investigation into their energy-conversion efficiency and energy-transformation properties. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. This user-friendly approach streamlines data analysis in real-time, expedites interpretation, and facilitates easy transition to high-throughput experiments from scanning modes. Furthermore, this approach allows users to take advantage of the significant speed gains provided by machine learning models. To illustrate this, we discuss our development of a collaborative workflow for automated, real-time analysis and processing of absorbance spectra acquired at the NSLS-II. This workflow demonstrates how machine learning models can be trained to recognize patterns in data from one beamline, with only limited extrapolation capability, as shown by our work at beamline NIU. Additionally, we highlight our establishment of a high-throughput experiment protocol for testing materials science models at the NSLS-II. This protocol leverages machine learning models to accelerate real-time analysis of images, scattering curves, and spectroscopy data acquired at the NSLS-II, specifically at beamlines NIU, NIW, and ENV. With this protocol, we successfully completed a series of high-throughput experiments at the NSLS-II, spanning over 50 unique materials science use cases and involving over 500 unique materials, with data analyzed in less than 5 minutes per scan. This work paves the way for the expansion of machine learning in user facilities, while also highlighting the potential of machine learning to accelerate research in materials science. As a result, we are launching a competition to develop new machine learning models for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the NSLS-II and encourage participation from both academic and industrial communities. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. Van Rhijn's life and work are reviewed in the course of this essay, with a focus on how his directorate both supported and hindered the advancement of the Selected Areas Plan. Despite the numerous obstacles he faced, van Rhijn maintained a steadfast commitment to achieving the plan's goals, eventually laying the groundwork for its successful realization over a decade after his death. This essay will be concluded with van Rhijn's own reflections on his time as director, as expressed through his own writings. Those personal accounts offer a unique insight into his thoughts on his tenure, his legacy, and the broader astronomical community he was a part of. Ultimately, this study provides a comprehensive examination of both van Rhijn's life and the historical context in which he operated, shedding new light on the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory and the Plan of Selected Areas. Adriaan Blaauw's own recollections and the archival records he left behind have been incorporated into this account, enriching our understanding of this pivotal period in the history of astronomy. This essay will be a valuable resource for anyone seeking to learn about the life and work of Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory, and the implementation of the Plan of Selected Areas. This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but resulted in increased early submission rates among transfer students. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. To further explore these findings, a survey was administered to gather students' subjective experiences with remote learning, revealing four key challenges - technical issues, time management, motivation, and financial constraints - that demographic groups faced at different rates. These results indicate the value of infrastructure investments to enhance technical capabilities, the need for flexible course schedules, and the importance of financial support to minimize students' financial constraints during remote learning. Moreover, the study proposes several innovative assessment tools to evaluate the effectiveness of remote learning experiences and course materials. Ultimately, the research underlines the significance of entailing diverse perspectives in the design of remote learning experiences and course assessments to promote equitable learning outcomes for all students. Finally, the study suggests several guidelines and practical recommendations for educators, course designers, and institutional policymakers to create more adaptable and student-centered remote learning experiences. These guidelines can facilitate smooth academic transitions for students during periods of disruption caused by global crises and other transitional periods. Additionally, the study provides statistical support for the benefits of diversifying online learning platform interfaces to promote more inclusive and accessible learning experiences. Nonetheless, the study concludes that more substantial evidence is required to fully validate its findings

However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. The algorithm is highly flexible, allowing easy integration with other preconditioning methods, and its scalability makes it suitable for big data applications. The nested implementation of the Neumann Series provides a general framework that extends to higher-order iterations, and we provide a publicly accessible GPU-enabled matrix inversion library called 'NN-GL' to facilitate easy usage of the NN method. The experimental evaluations conducted on a range of linear systems and matrix inversion benchmarks have shown excellent performance on real and synthetic datasets across various problem sizes and conditions. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the NN method with respect to other state-of-the-art fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. The research introduces an open research question regarding the potential extension of the nested approach to other mathematical operations such as singular value decomposition. The study concludes by outlining the potential applications of the NN method to other domains and the scope for further research on the proposed approach. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that our model can be experimentally realized using an optical lattice setup with binary disorders. This setup involves simultaneously controlling two random potential patterns, achieved through the use of random binary strains in lead chalcogenide materials. These materials exhibit a large linear contrast between the sizes of the local unit cells, enabling a topological Anderson insulating phase to be directly observed through mean winding number, mean chiral amplitude, and mean on-site energy. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of topological Anderson insulators in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders.

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. These discrepancies stem from variations in network protocols used, leading to potential network noise and scalability limitations.
This study assesses the performance, scalability, and cost implications of running HPC applications on cloud infrastructure.
Initially, the investigation focuses on latency, bandwidth, and data transfer patterns in small-scale tests, followed by simulations on a larger scale.
Validation is conducted across multiple cloud providers and HPC systems, revealing that system noise and variability can substantially impact both performance and cost at both small and large scales. 
Ultimately, the research finds that system noise can significantly reduce the efficiency of large-scale HPC deployments in the cloud. 
To mitigate this, a method is proposed to reduce system noise by allocating an additional node with a 20% increase in cost. 
This enhanced approach yields improved performance, scalability, and cost efficiency in cloud-based HPC applications. 
The proposed method is shown to result in a 5x performance improvement, a 20x scalability enhancement, and a 0.4x cost reduction compared to the baseline in certain scenarios. 
These findings are applicable to various HPC applications and could be adapted to other use cases with network-intensive characteristics. 
The proposed method may also be relevant to on-premise HPC deployments that utilize cloud-like network architectures. 
Overall, this study highlights the importance of considering system noise and variability when designing and optimizing cloud-based HPC systems. 
It further introduces a novel approach to handle noise, which could be a valuable contribution to existing research in this area. 
However, it is essential to note that this study is a preliminary investigation, and there is a clear need for more in-depth research on this subject.

Lastly, the proposed method could be examined for its potential to benefit other technology areas that rely on HPC systems and cloud infrastructure.
