A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. This research offers insights into controlling legged robots on soft ground and suggests ways to enhance their stability. Additionally, the project showcases an interesting connection between the RFT model and the robot's feedback controller. This connection creates an intriguing phenomenon where the robot's controller effectively utilizes the RFT model's limitations to achieve better performance. This relationship could be explored to develop more effective control systems for robots moving on soft ground by intentionally introducing a similar foot size to grain diameter ratio in future studies. This model's simplicity makes it an suitable example for teaching control system fundamentals through simulation. This research is an extension of previous work presented at the 2018 ASME Dynamic Systems and Control Conference. Significant revisions have been made since then, including the addition of numerical results obtained with a numerical solution to the robot's dynamics, the inclusion of additional figures, and a clearer explanation of the discrete element method simulation. These changes have resulted in a more comprehensive paper that provides an overview of modeling, simulation, and control of a one-legged hopping robot on soft ground. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our expectations are that these challenging datasets and evaluation protocols will push the limits of current NLP models and our results from extensive experiments conducted across five different models definitely validate these expectations. Most importantly, our CONDAQA dataset proves that substantial gaps continue to exist between human performance and that of state-of-the-art NLP models in the complex task of reasoning about negation. As a result, we strongly believe that this dataset will serve as a pivotal reference point for all future work aimed at closing this gap through the development of more sophisticated NLP models. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the potential for dynamical learning of quantum systems' behavior during quenching to enhance the performance of quantum annealing algorithms. Due to the general nature of these conclusions, they are likely to be applicable to a broad spectrum of problems solvable via quantum annealing. extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Ultimately, this study shows that understanding the intricate physics of infinite
niobate and cobaltate materials requires careful consideration of correlation
strength and the relative filling of the $s$ and $d$ orbital types. 
Consequently, these findings are relevant to research on heavy $f$-electron
superconductors in narrow bands and the complex physics of transition metal
oxides. 
In addition, this study highlights an intriguing connection between
self-doped materials and the Kondo-lattice effect, shedding new light on the
physics underlying infinite layered nickelates and cobaltates.

by both analytical modeling and experimental research.

The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time. This computational complexity matches the time complexity of the original Tai mapping problem when both trees are ordered. We believe our solution contributes a significant improvement to recent integer programming approaches for the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem. We implemented our algorithm in a source code available upon request. We took advantage of this algorithm to set new upper bounds for the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem on some benchmark instances. Our results show that our algorithm's output sometimes outperforms the state-of-the-art integer programming solvers in terms of solution quality, despite sometimes failing to find a feasible solution while the original instance is known to be feasible. We suspect this failure arises from the absence of an underlying logic in our algorithm to ensure that all nodes in one tree will be matched with corresponding nodes in the second tree. We visually illustrate our algorithm's efficiency through an animated GIF available online. We experimentally evaluated our algorithm on randomly generated unordered trees. Our results indicate that its running time matches the predicted $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time complexity. Building on the SSMLearn algorithm, which applies implicit optimization to fit a system's underlying structure to available data and simplifies the systems' dynamics, we have created two more direct methods that transform the process into explicit problems under specific assumptions. These algorithms demonstrate the ability to create precise and highly simplified models for complex systems on both numerical and real-world datasets, significantly reducing the computational time. Additionally, these models exhibit exceptional performance in predicting future system values and comparing the dimensionality of the systems' underlying structure. 

The three algorithms we have created are currently available on the Los Alamos National Adams repository. Our work has also inspired a novel application in identifying the number of modes in a system's underlying structure, a crucial but often unknown value.

This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. To illustrate the practical applicability of SIMC 2.0, we successfully implement a working prototype and demonstrate its effectiveness with real-world ML models. Additionally, our formal security analysis and protocol evaluation verify the security and efficacy of SIMC 2.0 in various scenarios. Finally, we explore potential optimizations and identify areas for further development to bridge the gap between current efficient secure protocols and the high-performance, commercially viable solutions. To this end, we propose an open challenge to the research community to address two key challenges in securing ML inference protocols. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/weizheng1123/SIMC2.0. Leveraging the efficient design of the protocol, we also introduce a novel application called "Efficient Medication Adherence Management" and present the methodology and results of a user study featuring real participants. The incorporation of our high-performance protocol leads to a significant increase in user satisfaction by at least 2.5 times. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for the development of low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries. Additionally, these devices may enable the creation of miniaturized point-spectral analyzers for use in spacecraft and telescopes, enhancing our understanding of the cosmos. Overall, this technology marks a significant breakthrough in the field of spectrographic technology.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. Additionally, a variant called delayed random walk learning is introduced and shown to be robust to extreme data heterogeneity, resulting in faster convergence and better model performance. Finally, our findings are verified through simulations and real-world experiments on multiple large-scale datasets. A novel application of random walk learning is also presented, along with its execution on a substantial healthcare graph. The proposed algorithms are available open-source at https://github.com/hjchaisen/FEDRW. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  However, the research acknowledges limitations in its ability to establish a causal link between mental health treatment and a decrease in future crime due to potential biases in the data set used.  Notably, the court cases used in this study already established a link between mental health and future crime and focused on individuals who were sentenced to non-prison sentences, who represent a smaller percentage of North Carolina's inmate population.  As such, the findings may not be directly applicable to all individuals within the state's inmate population.  To build upon these findings, the authors suggest several potential modifications to the research design, including the use of administrative data sets that cover a broader time frame and more diverse population of convicted individuals.  These data sets include the North Carolina Department of Correction's inmate population and the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services' mental health treatment providers. To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This ATCA board utilizes an array of components such as electrical-optical devices and multi-gigabit transceivers for data transfer, as well as a custom 24-layer PCB to minimize interference while maintaining high signal integrity. This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 12.8 gigabits per second during in-house and CERN integrated testing. With production scheduled for completion by the end of 2018, the full jFEX system will be ready for deployment before the LHC's anticipated 2021 restart. This project has also established valuable collaborations between industrial companies and research institutions that will be vital for its ongoing support and future maintenance requirements. This project is part of the ATLAS upgrade program, where its successful outcome will serve as a model for implementing other complex detector systems. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. This work also expands our understanding of floating rafts by showing that the reassembly of particles in this context is governed not just by forces like viscosity and surface tension but also the fluid dynamics of the surrounding liquid. The result of this research could be applied to other situations where materials are broken down, like the formation of cracks in thin layers of ice or soap films. Additionally, the reassembly of particles in these situations could be used to measure the surface tension of fluids with high precision. Finally, the fact that we can control the size of clusters within a raft by adjusting the rate at which we stretch it may also provide a useful model for exploring the balance between order and disorder in materials. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive and efficient circuits for sorting. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Through our research, we found lower bounds on the comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with constant depth. Rounding is an essential concept used extensively in research, yet its implications on discrete random variables have not been extensively explored. To understand changes in rare events such as suicides, officials may release rounded statistics of deaths, which can distort the actual findings if rates are already low. In this research, we focus on estimating non-negative discrete variables using rounded averages, specifically looking at the impact on Poisson random counts. Our analysis explores the effects of rounding on the mean, distribution, and most importantly, the likelihood of specific events occurring. We also discuss the statistical implications of releasing rounded data from independent samples, including the impact on testing the difference in event rates. Our results show that when rounding is random, it acts as an extra source of error in testing independent populations, but does not reduce the effectiveness of tests when comparing the same population at different time points. However, our most critical finding is that it significantly hampers the ability to detect changes in low-probability events, actually making it more difficult with full knowledge of the rounding method. Our analysis also offers strategies for coping with this issue, primarily by suggesting methods for incorporating the variance of the rounding process and alternative approaches for analyzing data, such as using distribution transformations. Ultimately, our research confirms the widespread concern that releasing rounded statistics can conceal meaningful changes in rare events. Our analysis is relevant to any setting where statistical estimates are subject to systematic variation due to rounding, common in business, economics, medicine, and social sciences. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the presence of a spin singlet ground state was confirmed by isothermal magnetization in high magnetic fields. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in GdInO3, contradicting the expectations of researchers. This phenomenon was explained by incorporating a minor amount of oxygen vacancies, which results in a more disordered state and increased magnetic moment of the Gd3+ ions. A method of calculating the effective spin frustration factor (ggS) was established through a combined analysis of the unique magnetic properties of the triangular and honeycomb sublattices. The value of ggS was found to be 1.34, indicating strong spin frustration in GdInO3. A semi-analytical approach combined with finite-size and anisotropy effects was used to explain the magnetic phase transitions and entropy changes. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This typically involves fine-tuning the method using the target domain's unlabeled training data in order to achieve good results. This paper presents an original model that uses a unique threshold measurement formula in the Realized-GARCH model. The new framework utilizes a non-linear model that takes into account the 'leverage effect' and models the connection between realized volatility and hidden volatility. A specific estimation method was adopted, a simulation test was performed to evaluate its effectiveness. Furthermore, the paper conducts a practical study using real-world data, predicting Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall for various stock market indices with varying forecasting lengths. Results demonstrate the capability of the new framework to achieve competitive accuracy compared to established GARCH and Realized-GARCH type models. 

### Abstract

A novel framework based on the Realized-GARCH model has been developed, distinguished by its exclusive use of a new threshold measurement formula. Specifically, the model employs the Minimal Realized Volatility (MRV) approach, where the hidden volatility is set as the minimum value between the realized volatility and a function of the previous day's volatility. Unlike the traditional ARCH model, where the square of the volatility is modeled, the MRV framework models the logarithm of the volatility. To estimate the parameters of the model, a Bayesian method was adopted, over-sampling being utilized to enhance estimation efficiency. A simulation test confirmed the effectiveness of this estimation approach. Moreover, the paper conducts a practical study on tail risk forecasting for major global stock market indices using real-world data, the results showing the new framework outperforms established GARCH and Realized-GARCH type models. Notably, the model exhibits superior performance in forecasting the tail risk of the global stock market portfolio.

The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Model simulations of correlation functions that incorporate a significant contribution from the quark--antiquark correlation are shown to align well with our lattice data when analyzed within the context of a specific mass window. Nonetheless, the data outside of this mass range suggests that the quark--antiquark correlation's influence requires more detailed scrutiny. Our study lays the groundwork for further investigations of the quark's spin-dependent properties and its interactions within hadrons. Our method introduces a new, effective approach for evaluating the physical properties of hadrons via correlation functions of quark currents, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the role of quark--antiquark correlations in the behavior of hadrons. This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US. 

In contrast to previous laboratory research finding a stronger desire to eliminate differences when luck's impact is limited, our findings indicate that participants show a weaker response in scenarios where luck's impact is widespread. This reduction in response is seen as a key factor explaining the greater inequality observed in laboratory settings compared to real-world data, which does show a relationship between luck's influence and observed inequality levels. 

To further investigate this discrepancy, we conducted additional research to see if varying aspects of the laboratory environment, such as pay rates and stakes, could influence participants' responses to scenarios where luck has an impact on job outcomes. However, we found no evidence that these changes affect the results, which suggests that the observed effect holds consistently across different laboratory settings. 

The final section of the study explores policy implications, specifically looking at the impact of different measures designed to counter the limited attention people tend to give to luck's influence on job success. One approach aims to raise awareness about the chances influencing outcomes by informing participants about the underlying probability distributions, while the other seeks to frame job success in relation to broader income distribution. Our results show that participants responding to the second approach exhibit increased desire for income redistribution, which suggests it to be an effective strategy in addressing the limited attention people give to luck's impact on job success. 

On the other hand, informing participants about the probability distributions does not raise their perceived inequality levels or increase their desire to redistribute income. This finding implies that people's limited attention to luck's influence on job success cannot be overcome by simply providing them with more accurate information about chance influencing job outcomes. 

In conclusion, our research confirms that people generally want to reduce income inequality but finds a crucial limitation in this desire. It reveals a significant disparity between laboratory research and real-world data on inequality trends in the US, explaining the observed difference as being due to the specific way luck influences job success in laboratory settings. It also explores policy implications aimed at addressing this limitation by testing different approaches to counter the effect

This action induces a mapping $\pi : X \to X'$ between corresponding flag varieties, which essentially discards information to yield a coarser partial flag structure in $X'$. In a context of stable maps, for sufficiently large degrees, a key geometric object - associated with maps that target Schubert varieties $X_i$ - exhibits the structure of a rational connection over its parameter space in $X'$, which now reflects maps targeting $\pi(X_i)$. By examining a universal hyperplane arrangement $Fl_{1,n-1}$ and the behavior of maps onto it, we are also able to identify relationships in its quantum $K$-ring through a geometric, analytical approach that includes Chevalley's theorem. Additionally, our methods allow us to prove a related conjecture involving the Hodge number of certain manifolds. 

In the case of Grassmannians $Gr_{1,n-1}$, we find that its quantum $K$-ring can be expressed as the ring of a specific type of polynomial, whose variables represent Schubert classes and are related to plucker classes by means of mutations. Our findings on the equivariant quantum $K$-ring of flag varieties have been previously noted by Hopkins and Strickland in their work on further extending the Adams isomorphism. 

Our approach to studying the quantum $K$-ring of flag varieties has been influenced by the Adams isomorphism and its extension to a context of finite fields. Our results, particularly those involving the ring structure of quantum $K$-rings, suggest connections to a broader theory of extended Adams isomorphisms. 

In the case of the universal hyperplane arrangement $Fl_{1,n-1}$, we are able to express its extended Adams isomorphism as a relation involving the self-intersection of a specific divisor. This relation, in turn, provides insight into the structure of its quantum $K$-ring. 

Our findings on the universal hyperplane arrangement $Fl_{1,n-1}$ can be applied to examine the extended Adams isomorphism in contexts of partial flags based on projective space and defined over a field of the form $F_{q}$, whose characteristic is not 2.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings. DataScope's efficient algorithms for computing the Shapley value are expected to pave the way for the practical implementation of data debugging in various machine learning applications. The system's source code is available at https://github.com/mitnlp/datadebugging/. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The code for our method is available at https://github.com/UMHLab/SIT. The GAT-based approach we explored faces an excessive computational burden, thus we introduce an alternative, efficient variant called Efficient Shared Individual Trajectories (E-SIT), which achieves comparable performance at a significantly lower cost. In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from single-particle entanglement surpasses classical explanation and contributes to its unique characteristics. Furthermore, this phenomenon enables truly non-local effects, such as single-particle steering, which can only be achieved by incorporating the instantaneous non-locality of single-particle entanglement. As a result, we propose that the spread of the entangled wave function serves as an indication of the instantaneous non-local phenomenon. Finally, we examine the instantaneous non-locality of single-particle entanglement in the context of the Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen state and show that it is directly related to the steering of this state. Nevertheless, the instantaneous non-locality of single-particle entanglement can still be sustained even in the absence of a classical communication channel, as demonstrated by our reconstruction of the Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen experiment using single-particle entanglement. Furthermore, over extended periods, the spreading of the entangled wave function resulting from single-particle entanglement can give rise to a quantum non-locality that exceeds classical explanation and contributes to its unique characteristics. In quantum computing, generating the entanglement of any number of qubits in a single operation has significant implications for error correction, particularly when combined with stabilizer measurements. Utilizing a single multi-qubit gate instead of several two-qubit gates in parity-check circuits is demonstrated using the toric code, resulting in improved fault tolerance when applying a five-qubit gate over individual two-qubit gates in the context of quantum error correction, particularly when applied to ion qubits susceptible to spontaneous photon scattering, leading to an approximate $40\%$ threshold advantage in the latter case. Furthermore, this research shows that the advantage holds even when qubit loss is considered the dominant error source. Although the benefit may not translate to all quantum error correction protocols, this study highlights the potential value of examining qubit-gate-specific metrics in optimization tasks. Additionally, this research facilitates the utilization of five-qubit gates over two-qubit gates in the toric code, achieving a $40\%$ better fault-tolerant quantum error threshold in the case of ion qubits. This involves executing the following sequence of operations: (1) apply a single multi-qubit gate instead of multiple two-qubit gates for qubit entanglement; (2) perform parities by measuring the stabilizer operators consisting of the tensor product of single-qubit Pauli X operators; (3) execute the multi-qubit gate in the correct order to ensure correct decoding; (4) apply the correct Pauli X gate to the appropriate qubits based on the fusion table resulting from the multi-qubit gate; (5) repeat steps 2-4 for each multi-qubit gate in the circuit before moving on to the final measurement. This approach yields two benefits: (1) executing a single multi-qubit gate rather than multiple two-qubit gates reduces the total number of gate operations required; (2) however, this also introduces the risk of qubit loss during the execution of the multi-qubit gate, which further decreases the reliable execution rate of the code and necessitates a longer period of running the fault-tolerant protocol. This trade-off holds for all quantum error correction protocols that rely on qubit entanglement, as executing a single multi-qubit gate rather than multiple two-qubit gates is necessary. This research provides a framework for addressing this issue, as it paves the way for the development of more complex multi-qubit gates in the toric code, which is a crucial step in large-scale quantum computing applications. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry and feedback the index. Feedback encoding is accomplished by comparing received signals with GMM components, ultimately selecting the most representative one and returning its index. Based on received feedback, the base station determines an appropriate precoder and codebook entry, and sends it to the mobile terminal. Uplink transmission utilizes the identified precoder and codebook entry. The proposed approach enhances performance compared to conventional methods in scenarios employing frequency-division duplex (FDD) systems. Moreover, the codebook construction method exhibits superior adaptability in scenarios employing time-division duplex (TDD) systems. The approach may result in increased computational complexity during training the GMM, but overall it offers improved performance across both duplex modes. A numerical study using 5G wireless communication standards validates the effectiveness of the proposed approach. A developed code block transmission (CBT) protocol based on GMMs outperforms conventional protocols by approximately 5 dB in data transfer rate in an FDD system. The findings are applicable to a wide range of wireless communication systems employing feedback communication. A key shortcoming of the proposed approach is the potential for reduced diversity when using a single feedback channel, although this issue is being addressed through the development of an enhanced code block transmission protocol. Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a corresponding hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. Overall, this research provides a pioneering example of a co-designed LSTM framework that addresses the challenges associated with high-performance video recognition and may serve as a reference for the development of other compressed machine learning models. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation may play a significant role in quantum double dark-soliton dynamics, and that states with high condensate fractions should be well-represented by a quasi-condensation state that follows a mean-field model. Current constraints from Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis already set a strict limit on their lifespan, at under 0.1 seconds. Next-generation gravitational wave detectors have the potential to drastically improve these limits to the point where their lifespan could be constrained to as short as 10^-16 seconds. This could be possible if these particles once controlled the universe's energy density and led to a transition to a matter-dominated period before decaying in time for Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis to occur. As a result of such an early history of the universe, we could detect unique signatures in gravitational wave backgrounds that originated from primordial sources. Furthermore, we propose that detecting the gravitational wave spectrum from long-lived objects like cosmic strings can serve as a probe of fundamental particle physics parameters, ultimately providing more stringent constraints on the universe's early conditions through various model's theoretical predictions, especially in the case of the minimal supersymmetric standard model, its minimal flavoured version, and certain models of universal extra dimensions, among others. By changing the swimmer body and its helical tail dimensions, our findings reveal that viscoelastic properties' influence is largely dependent on the swimmer design, potentially amplifying its speed by as much as five times, or instead, diminish its velocity by a similar amount, or leave its locomotion mostly unaffected. Analysis and corresponding theoretical modeling suggest that viscoelastic forces on these swimmers are dictated by a similar'snowman effect' found with linear swimmers, in which asymmetry in the swimmer causes an elasticity-related force that may aid or impede propulsion. This idea is visually represented with our model's 'asymmetry factor' ($\cal A$), determined by measuring the helical tail's cross-sectional area, and demonstrates its applicability to an broad range of swimmers, suggesting its utility in guiding the design of viscoelastic swimming devices. Additionally, our research offers evidence that viscoelastic fluids' behavior in controlled experiments can be complex and influenced by the presence of air, requiring careful consideration in similar studies. The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. The code is openly accessible at https://github.com/tuoyang116/ASSIST, encouraging the use of pseudo labels in other challenging NLP tasks. The model performance on testing sets with little or no noise is also presented in the study. The results show that although the models achieve good performance on unseen data, they still struggle with certain types of user requests and failed book appointments, indicating areas for future research to further improve dialogue state tracking. The obtained model models have been submitted to the official evaluation servers for reference. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. To address this shortcoming, the model is modified to incorporate a non-local fraction of " Nomadic" individuals who are more prone to engaging in destructive behavior and are distributed unevenly across Santiago. Furthermore, the updated model highlights the significant impact of "Nomadic" individuals on both the temporal and spatial dimensions of the disorders. The model's enhanced spatial capabilities indicate that it is capable of accurately capturing the city's underlying social structure and may be adapted to forecast potential disorderly scenarios and evaluate policy interventions aimed at preventing or mitigating the spread of violence. The model is also shown to be robust and reliable in its predictions, indicating that it may be applicable to other similar episodes of urban unrest. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose graphic illustrations to visualize these scenarios and find that hybrid models containing both prescriptions can still exhibit local polarity reversals at specific latitudes.

Ultimately, we conclude that stars exhibiting anti-solar differential rotation can only support magnetic cycles under highly specific dynamo processes. As a result, observational indicators of magnetic cycles, such as X-ray emission and chromospheric network development, may be used to map the rotational evolution of solar-type stars and potentially identify slow rotators that have already entered the post-main sequence phase. Additionally, these findings imply that stars with anti-solar differential rotation may never display the rotational evolution characteristic of solar-type stars. As these stars spend a considerable amount of time on the main sequence, broad population synthesis simulations are essential to understand the broader implications of this phenomenon. A crucial boundary, the quantum null energy condition, is used to measure the change in a region's entanglement entropy along a null direction in order to understand the quantum thermodynamics of complex systems. Investigating whether the quantum null energy condition limits irreversible entropy generation during quenching driven by an influx of energy and momentum from an infinite, memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories, our research finds that an increase in both entropy and temperature, as required by the classical Clausius inequality, is necessary to prevent a violation of the quantum null energy condition, specifically in quenching transitions that result in changes in thermal states dual to Banados-Teitelboim-Zanelli geometries. Additionally, our research provides lower and upper bounds for the change in entropy or temperature for a specific change in temperature or entropy in any initial state. Furthermore, our results indicate that the null energy condition is never overstepped in time and that the asymptotic rates can be determined analytically. Our study demonstrates that the entanglement entropy within a region of a specific length, $l$, eventually reaches a steady-state within a time frame of $l/2$ with an exponential decay rate of $3/2$, and that the coefficient for the quadratic growth of entanglement in time can be found for any $l$, and that the asymptotic rate of growth for a semi-infinite interval is directly proportional to the difference of the entropy densities of the initial and final states, along with determining the upper and lower limits for these rates of growth. Our research also shows that the asymptotic rate of growth for an exponential increase of proportionality to $l^{2}$ is directly proportional to $l^{2}$ and that the asymptotic rate of growth for an exponential increase of proportionality to $e^{x}$ is directly proportional to $e^{x}$, and that the asymptotic rate of growth for a logarithmic increase is directly proportional to the coefficient of the quadratic growth of entanglement in time, and that the asymptotic rate of growth for a linear increase in time is directly proportional to the ratio of the entropy to the temperature of the system. Our research provides theoretical evidence that the quantum null energy condition acts as an bound on the growth of entanglement in time following a quench. and that this bound is necessary in order to prevent a violation of the quantum null energy condition, and that it is possible to understand the quantum thermodynamics of complex systems through the measurement of a crucial boundary, the quantum null energy condition.

We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. We also show that these bounds apply equally to the optimal time to release a two-level system and multiple-level systems. Furthermore, we find that the optimal time to release a two-level system or a Landau-Zener model corresponds to a specific point on the boundary of the Bloch ball. These findings contribute to our understanding of quantum state evolution and the interplay between unitary and non-unitary processes. Moreover, they demonstrate that asymptotic bounds on quantum state evolution can be very tight and provide new insights into the optimal time to release a two-level system or a Landau-Zener model. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Additionally, we explore methods to enhance the visibility of spatial variations in carrier concentrations using a larger terahertz spot size or carrier dynamics manipulation. These findings are relevant to any microwave device operating at cryogenic temperatures and could be adapted to devices utilizing niobium or silicon-based superconducting quantum processors.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This work is part of the ongoing interdisciplinary study on the interior of Venus, with an emphasis on the atmosphere's evolution and future prospects. This review is part of a broader compilation of chapters that will be published as a comprehensive reference on the interior of Venus. This report will be made available at the website of the Venus Exploration Working Group. High-resolution figure images and additional information about the processes and feedback mechanisms of the interior of Venus can be found in the supplemental materials of this article. The success of cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcomes depends heavily on the properties and spatial organization of cells within tissues. Therefore, computer-assisted cancer care relies heavily on accurate representations of tissues that can capture key histological details. Building upon existing cell-graphs that encode cell characteristics and spatial relationships, researchers have been using machine learning to establish correlations between tissue structure and function. However, a single cell-centric approach falls short of describing the complex hierarchical organization within tissues. In response, a novel multi-scale graph representation of tissues has been proposed, comprising of multiple layers of histological entities, along with their relationships. A corresponding graph neural network is also proposed, allowing tissue structure to be linked to its functional behavior. Specifically, this method utilizes cell and tissue region features extracted from histology images to create HierArchical Cell-to-Tissue graphs. An associated neural network is designed to classify such graph representations, referred to as HACT-Net. As part of this work, a comprehensive dataset called the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset is created and employed to evaluate the efficacy of this method against pathologist assessments and current approaches. Experimental studies demonstrate the superiority of this method over alternative techniques and even expert pathologist assessments in breast tumor subtyping tasks. Furthermore, this method is adaptable to other tasks by simply updating the classifier layer, showcasing its efficient combination of cancer-specific knowledge and general neural network capabilities. Comprehensive evaluations using comprehensive quantitative and qualitative assessments provide insight into the strengths and limitations of this method. Additionally, a discussion on the implications of using this method for the clinical community is included, highlighting the need for low-cost, reproducible, and scalable approaches that this method efficiently addresses. Furthermore, this method is deemed suitable for integrating multiple imaging modalities due to its flexible layer structure, representing a promising direction for future research. As the smallest unit used in this method represents a cluster of cells rather than individual cells, it may be necessary in future iterations to incorporate a higher resolution layer within this architecture. Moreover, the relatively small sample size of the BRACS dataset compared to other publicly available datasets may not be sufficient for modeling certain aspects of tissue structures. Consequently, creating larger, publicly available datasets such as the BRACS dataset is essential to develop accurate models of tissue structures. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. This is accompanied by a discussion on the methodical use of suitable prior distributions to achieve this consistency. Finally, our findings on Bayesian estimation and graph consistency are complemented by a discussion on the limitations and challenges of the current approach. To facilitate thorough investigation, we also report on the results of a novel dataset analyzing earthquake occurrences in Italy. All the analysis code is openly accessible for reproduction of the results. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM. We demonstrate the method's efficacy through pairwise and single-step algorithm tests, showcasing minimal performance differences. In contrast, the standard FMM method exhibits significant angular momentum disruption in high velocity and mass ratio scenarios. Despite slight increases in operation costs, our method offers superior accuracy. Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached optimal performance in medical image segmentation, the process is hindered by a large number of required annotations for training. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotated datasets of similar anatomical structures for training. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-anatomy domains due to differences in image modalities and target structures' appearance. To overcome this, we propose Contrastive Semi-Supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that allows a model to segment similar structures in a target domain with only a limited number of target domain annotations, aided by existing annotations in a source domain. We employ Domain-Specific Batch Normalization to normalize anatomical feature maps from the two domains separately, introduce a cross-domain contrastive learning approach to promote extracting domain-invariant features, and integrate these into a Self-Ensembling Mean-Teacher (SE-MT) framework that leverages unlabeled target domain images and incorporates prediction consistency constraints. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the CS-CADA's ability to solve the complex cross-anatomy domain shift issue, resulting in the accurate segmentation of coronary arteries in X-ray images, aided by retinal vessel images, and cardiac MR images, aided by fundus images, with only a limited number of target domain annotations. The project includes thorough experimentation and comparison of multiple state-of-the-art SSL approaches, demonstrating its applicability and practical value for real-world medical image segmentation challenges. The code is available at https://github.com/zhm-sjtu/CS-CADA. The model achieves notable improvements over the baseline model, reducing the performance gap caused by limited target domain annotations by approximately 20%. The project's findings provide significant insight into solving the complex problem of cross-anatomy domain adaptation, making it applicable to various medical image segmentation tasks. A straightforward examination indicates that this 1.5 order formalism is inherently defective in all contexts. Although it appears that the associated algebra is closed, a detailed examination in a simplified setting reveals the presence of a non-nilpotent BRS operator generated by the 1.5 order formalism. Consequently, this is also applicable to supergravity, suggesting the necessity of formulating revised nilpotent transformations to accurately comprehend 3+1 dimensional supergravity. A potential approach to achieve this is by supplementing the auxiliary fields to incorporate the spin connection within a super Yang-Mills multiplet. This revised interpretation of the 1.5 order formalism is then consistent with the principles of local supersymmetry. A key aspect of this revised formulation is the redefinition of the supercurrent, which is now expressed in terms of the spin connection and a super transformation of the super Yang-Mills multiplet. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. Additionally, its ability to effectively handle short pulses makes it a useful tool for the development of novel higher-energy x-ray sources and particle acceleration techniques. Furthermore, its potential to deliver high-powered pulses with specific temporal and spatial characteristics increases its value in the advancement of experimental methods used in high-energy density physics and laser-plasma interactions. Two possible designs for this component are also introduced, encompassing a basic thin film as well as a stacked layer structure, both capable of executing this function. These designs provide a foundation for the development of more complex devices, such as switches and modulators, which depend on the same principle of operation. These potential applications, coupled with the capability of this type of plasma waveplate to handle multiple cycle periods, make it an essential component for the effective utilization of laser systems that produce pulses of one to ten cycle durations. This includes novel high-power laser systems based on optical parametric amplification, such as the OLED technique. Furthermore, this component is also suitable for systems that generate very short pulses, such as few-femtosecond second harmonic generation systems. It is essential to note that while this type of plasma waveplate offers significant advantages over traditional solid-state optics, its implementation depends on the development of advanced magnetic field control systems capable of managing the field in the plasma accurately. Nonetheless, the potential benefits it provides for the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems make it an important area of research. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. We experimentally verify the effectiveness of these ideas on a variety of rank metric code constructions. 

For code rates less than half, we further demonstrate that many classical lattice constructions can resist rank metric attacks capable of up to n-k error rank. Additionally, we propose a new code construction that combines elements from both matrix and vector code architectures, thereby achieving better error correction performance than code equivalents in the binary Hamming metric. This new code construction retains most of the efficient decoding benefits characteristic of vector code constructions. 

Lastly, we explore potential extensions to our techniques for use with other distance metrics, such as the minimum rank distance. We conclude that our proposed decoding strategies can significantly enhance the performance of rank metric codes in various applications. Additionally, our work lays the foundation for further research into the intersection of rank metric codes and topics like cryptology, secure multi-party computation, and code-based cryptography. Finally, we suggest that our new code constructions and decoding methods could be adapted for use in other error correcting schemes, such as lattice codes. 

We investigate the performance benefits of our proposed decoding strategies, which result in a marked improvement in error correction capacity over standard rank metric decoding approaches. In certain scenarios, our codes even outperform code equivalents constructed using the same generator matrices in the binary Hamming metric. Moreover, our code constructions and decoding strategies can tackle higher error grades than their binary Hamming metric counterparts. In some instances, our codes can correctly decode errors that cannot be corrected in the binary Hamming metric. 

We experimentally validate the performance benefits of our proposed decoding strategies on a variety of rank metric code constructions. In particular, we find that our diversity class of rank metric codes can accurately decode symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, even those of maximal rank, and that this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half.
